items.speaker: S01
items.quote: i think... it's different for me, and i'm not sure i like what i'm realizing about it. nameref is saying he'd need it to connect to who he already is, and that makes sense. nameref 's saying the structure around him won't even let him believe in it properly. but i'm stuck somewhere else — i don't think i actually know who i am well enough to know what would connect. and maybe that's worse because it means i'm not even fighting against anything real. i'm just... empty in some way. like, if someone said to me "this will make you a better bloke," i might listen. but i'm not sure what that means for me. i don't have a clear picture of what i'm trying to be better at, or who i'm trying to be better for. nameref 's got the village keeping him in shape. nameref has got his wife, his mates, things that matter to him. but me — i've just drifted into a life and i'm not even sure anymore if the things in it are things i chose or things i just... fell into. so what would it take? i think i'd need to actually figure out what matters to me first. not in the abstract — like, what do i actually want out of my time? what am i trying to do or be? and i'm 53 and i'm not sure i know that. that feels like the real barrier, not whether plant-based fits or doesn't fit. it's that nothing really fits because i don't know what i'm trying to fit anything into. that's probably what i should be thinking about before i worry about what i'm eating.

items.speaker: S03
items.quote: um, i do occasionally eat plant based meals at home, but that's probably more by chance. it just happens that meal is plant based. it’s not because i've made a deliberate choice to go out and buy something that was plant based. um, so whether it's at home or out, i think it's down to taste. and the few times when i have tried plant based versions of particular dishes, they've just, they've just not tasted as good. and inevitably, they've probably been more expensive, whether that's something i've bought from the supermarket, or or i can't think i've tried a plant based meal out and out and about but at home certainly plant based foods have been more expensive and not tasted as good. so it would need to taste better and it will need to be an equivalent or lower price.

items.speaker: S01
items.quote: yeah, i agree. but in some point, sometimes it helps make actually like for example, if i follow halal diet because i am muslim, sometimes plant based foods having good choice for me when i go to a non-halal place. like, it is the easy option for me and just choosing them. yeah maybe name can be different and they can show how the manufacturing process and they can say different things, as you said.

items.speaker: S04
items.quote: for me it's pretty straightforward, honestly. at work i usually just bring something — a sandwich, bit of meat in it usually, something simple that doesn't take much thought. and at home it's just... whatever's easy to sort out, really. i eat meat most days — red meat probably a couple times a week, bit of chicken now and then. it's just what i've always done, and it's quick to cook. doesn't really feel like a decision, if that makes sense. it's just the default. i suppose if i'm going out to eat, then yeah, i think a bit more about it — what kind of place it is, what i'm in the mood for. but day to day? it's not something i'm weighing up or anything. it's just... what's available, what i can throw together in twenty minutes after work.

items.speaker: S02
items.quote: yeah. yeah, that's it exactly. permission to be normal. that's a good way of putting it. i mean, at my age — i'm 48 now — you notice it more. when you're younger you just do it without thinking about it, don't you? but now i'm aware of how much i actually need that. not in a dramatic way, but just... i can feel the difference in myself if i've not had it for a while. you get a bit tighter, a bit more on guard. with work, you've got to be competent, professional, whatever. at home with the family there's all the stuff that needs managing — i've got a grown-up kid and my wife's got her own things going on, and you're just... you're performing that role. and it's not fake, but it's not relaxed either. but with your mates, the ones you've known a long time, you don't have to explain yourself. you just are. and that's rare, isn't it? actually rare. i think as you get older you realise how much you need those moments to just not be thinking about what you're supposed to be doing or saying. just sitting there with someone who knows you and doesn't need you to be anything in particular. that's not nothing. that's actually what it's about.

items.speaker: S03
items.quote: i get what you're saying, nameref . and maybe you're right that waiting for perfect clarity is its own trap. but i'm not sure it's as straightforward as just speaking first and figuring it out after. because here's the thing — i don't think you can actually separate thinking from doing like that. not the way you're describing it. if i just go home and say something without knowing what i actually think, i'm not suddenly going to figure out what i think by saying it. i'm going to figure out what i think she wants me to think. i'm going to read her reaction and adjust. i'm going to manage the conversation in real time based on how she's responding, which is exactly what i've already been doing. that's not finding out what i think. that's just doing the same thing with sound coming out. nameref 's right about something. there's a difference between not having clarity and genuinely not knowing what you know. and i think i'm closer to the second one. i've shut myself down so much that i'm not sure i can just open my mouth and suddenly be authentic about it. i'll just be reactive instead. so yeah, maybe i do need to start somewhere. but i don't think the answer is speak first, think later. i think i need to actually sit with what i want before i can say it without just managing her reaction. that's not waiting for permission. that's... trying to get back to knowing myself. because if i don't know myself, then nothing i say is going to mean anything anyway.

items.speaker: S04
items.quote: yeah, the pub for me too. it's just the thing, isn't it? i've got a couple of spots i rotate through up here. one's literally five minutes from my house, so that's often the default just because it's easy. but there's another one a bit further out that's got a better atmosphere, better crowd, so we'll head there if we're making more of an evening of it. i'm with you lot on the ritual side of it — at forty you're not trying to impress anyone anymore. you just want to sit down with people you know and not have to think too hard about it. that's the appeal. the food thing, yeah, i've noticed that too. i'm not obsessive about it or anything, but you do start to pick up on the difference between somewhere that's actually put thought into what they're serving and somewhere that just... hasn't. i mean, i eat meat most days — few times a week at least — so i notice when it's done properly versus when it's not. it's not like i'm seeking it out deliberately, but when you've had a decent steak or sunday roast done right, you remember it. makes you a bit more aware the next time you're ordering, you know? but like you say, nameref , i'm not going out of my way to source everything perfectly or anything daft like that. it's just... if i'm going to eat something, might as well be something decent if it's there.

items.speaker: S05
items.quote: exactly, yeah. and i think there's actually something decent about it though, even if it sounds like just a limitation. like, i know the butcher — i've known him for years. i know roughly where the meat's come from, whether it's local stuff or whatever. it's not some abstract choice where you're just grabbing whatever's cheapest off the shelf. so yeah, there's less convenience, but there's also... you know what you're eating a bit better, i suppose. you're not just going through the motions with whatever's in the supermarket. and honestly, the meat tastes different when you know the person selling it to you and they actually know what they're talking about. that matters to me. don't get me wrong, it's not like i'm being noble about it or anything. if there was a tesco five minutes away i'd probably use it sometimes too. but the constraint thing — it's not all bad. you end up knowing your food better, knowing your community better through that. it's just... a different way of doing it.

items.speaker: S02
items.quote: i don't know if i can quite claim that, to be honest. because i've been sitting here saying i'm making a choice and i'm aware of it, but i'm not sure i'm actually as outside it as nameref 's managing to be. like, when i said earlier that plant-based would need to fit into my family meals, and that the pub thing would only work if it was just... normal food — i think i was doing something similar to what nameref 's doing. i was framing it as practical barriers, which they are. but underneath that, there's also this thing where i don't want it to feel like i'm making a statement, or making a change. i want plausible deniability, almost — the option to be there without having to own it as a choice i'm making. and that's not the same as being outside the anxiety. that's actually being in it, just sideways. nameref can say he eats meat and doesn't worry about what it means because it's just default for him. but when i'm talking about how plant-based would have to work, i'm kind of... i'm still worried about what it means? or at least i want to avoid having to think about that. i want it to just be food, not a decision. which is fair enough, but it's not the same as standing outside the whole dynamic. i'm still caught in it, i'm just trying to avoid noticing that i am.

items.speaker: S04
items.quote: yeah, i know what you mean. i've definitely felt that — like, going into a cafe on your own, sitting down with a coffee or whatever, there's this weird self-consciousness about it. you're kind of aware you're a bloke sat alone, and you're thinking... i dunno, are people thinking i'm a weirdo? or like, should i be doing something else? should i be meeting someone? it's mental really because it shouldn't matter, but it does. and you're right about the app thing solving it in a way — because you're not actually in the space, you're not being looked at. the choice happens in private, the eating happens in private. there's no... there's no eyes on you, you know? but that's exactly what we were saying is bad about it, isn't it? like, we were talking about losing connection, losing community, everything becoming transactional. and this is kind of the same trap — the thing that lets you escape the awkwardness, the social performance of being a bloke eating alone, is the same thing that's killing off the actual human spaces and the connections that go with them. it's like we're trapped either way. either you're in a space feeling self-conscious, or you're at home avoiding the whole thing and losing out on... whatever it is we're meant to be losing. the texture, like nameref said. the actual place.

items.speaker: S01
items.quote: yeah, i eat meat too — red meat, fish, all of that. but i think where i'd be different from you, nameref , is that in manchester you just end up eating a wider range of stuff without necessarily deciding to. like, i'll have my red meat and fish, but i might have a curry one night, thai food another, someone might suggest a japanese place... it's just what's around you, and you get used to it. i'm not overthinking it either, but my pattern's probably a bit different because of where i am. i eat meat regularly — two, three times a week, fish maybe twice — but there's also nights where you're just grabbing something else because that's what the group fancies, or that's what's convenient. it's not a conscious choice to diversify, it's just... that's what living somewhere with more options does to you. same with dairy, to be honest — i probably have it less often than you do. not because i've decided against it, but it's just not what i reach for as much. there's other stuff available, so it naturally balances out differently. i think what you're doing — knowing what works for you and sticking with it — that's fair enough. but it's interesting how much where you live actually shapes what you end up eating without you really thinking about it.

items.speaker: S04
items.quote: yeah, right. so this is going to sound like it's got nothing to do with what we've been talking about, but it actually does, i think. most days i just grab something quick, yeah. but when i see my old man — which isn't as often as it should be, that twenty minutes might as well be an hour when you're busy — we actually sit down and eat something together. and that's different, you know? it's not just about the food being better or whatever. it's that you're doing it with someone, there's a bit of attention there. and i think that connects to what nameref was saying, actually. because you can live somewhere for years, know all the people, have the routine all set up. but if you're eating alone most nights, if you're just grabbing whatever's easiest, that's — i don't know, that's a kind of loneliness in itself, isn't it? you're fed, but you're on your own. when i'm with my dad we might just have beans on toast or whatever, but it feels different because it's not just fuel. someone's checking in with you while you're doing it, you're talking about stuff. that matters more than i think people realise, especially as you get older. and i reckon that's what's underneath all this embedded stuff we've been on about — it's not just about people noticing you're there. it's about someone actually spending time with you. actually eating with you, or whatever the equivalent is. most of my mates, same thing — they'd rather grab something quick than sit down properly. but when we do actually get together, that's when it feels like something's happened, you know?

items.speaker: S04
items.quote: i hear what you're all saying, and i think... yeah, there is something to it. i didn't think there was much, to be honest — i said earlier it all seemed fairly straightforward where i am — but listening to nameref and nameref talk about it, i can see the point. i mean, i eat meat, it's just what i do. but nameref 's right — i've never really questioned it, and i've not pushed back when someone's made a joke about a vegetarian mate or whatever. i just let it slide, because it didn't affect me. what bothers me more, if i'm being honest, is the idea that eating meat is somehow tied up with being a proper man. that feels daft to me. it does. i've never been one for all that — the proving yourself business, the whole thing where you've got to eat a certain way to show you're a bloke. that's childish. you are what you are, you eat what you eat. there shouldn't need to be some performance around it. but nameref 's right too — if nobody says anything, it just carries on. and i suppose i've been one of those people who hasn't said anything. i've just gone along with it because it didn't inconvenience me. which is... well, it's not great, is it? if one of my mates said he didn't fancy the meat one night, i should be able to just say "fine, order what you want" without there being any... any weight to it. and i could do that. i just haven't had to think about whether i was doing it.

items.speaker: S02
items.quote: well, i think that retirement thing plays into it more than you might expect, actually. when i was working, you just grabbed what was there, didn't you. lunchtime, dinner — you weren't thinking too much about it. my wife would sort the main meal in the evening, and that was that. but now i've got time. i'm doing a bit more of the cooking myself, and i find myself thinking about it differently. not in some sort of... i don't know, preachy way or anything. just more aware of what we're eating, how often things come round. used to be meat three, four times a week, easy. now it's maybe once a month, sometimes less. but it's not like i woke up one day and decided to be vegetarian or anything daft like that. it just sort of happened when you've got time to think about it, and you're standing at the supermarket looking at what's actually going in the trolley. i suppose the money side of it comes into it too when you're retired. you're thinking, do i really need to spend that much on a piece of steak when there's other things that do just as well? you eat a meal, you move on. the next day you're hungry again anyway. so yeah — it's less about having strong feelings about it and more about just having the space to actually notice what you're doing instead of just grabbing the first thing.

items.speaker: S03
items.quote: yeah, i'd say the pub for me too, but it's... it's a bit different out here, i think. i mean, nameref 's right about it being the place where you naturally end up, but out in the village there isn't really anywhere else to go, is there? it's not so much a choice. there's the one pub, and that's it. you go there because what else are you going to do — drive twenty minutes to the next town? so it becomes less about picking somewhere nice and more just... necessary, i suppose. it's the default. but that said, he's spot on about what happens when you're actually there. same thing — you sit down, have a pint, catch up properly with people you've known for years. the lads i see, we've all been coming to the same place forever. the difference though is it serves a different function out here. it's not just a social spot, it's kind of the hub, you know? you bump into people, you hear what's going on in the village, it's where things get discussed. it's the only place people gather really. so it matters in a different way than maybe it does in the city where you've got options.

items.speaker: S01
items.quote: um, i'll go next. do you, oh, do you want to go next or me?

items.speaker: S05
items.quote: right, exactly. and i think that's the thing — it fills you up properly, like you said. that's part of why it stays the default, isn't it? you have a sandwich with meat in it at lunch, you're not hungry again two hours later. you have a salad instead and you're thinking about a snack by mid-afternoon. so you keep going back to what actually works. and then there's just... i dunno, it's familiar. you grow up eating a certain way, your mates eat the same way, it's what you cook at home because you know how to do it. so it becomes automatic. but underneath that automation there's actual reasons — it's satisfying, it's practical, you know what you're getting. so when you do choose it, you're choosing it for reasons that make sense, even if you're not spelling them out every time you do it. that's probably why it doesn't feel like a big decision. because it kind of isn't one in the moment — you just grab what works. but the habit itself, that's built on real things, not just... mindlessness.

items.speaker: S03
items.quote: yeah, i'd say that's pretty much where i'm at too, but i think there's maybe a bit more to it than just convenience, you know? like, nameref 's right that it's practical — cost is massive for me, honestly. meat's often the cheapest protein you can get, especially if you're just grabbing something quick. red meat's usually decent value compared to other stuff, fish can be pricey. so that shapes what i actually end up eating more than anything else probably. but i don't think that means it's not deep, if that makes sense? like, people talk about food decisions like they're just surface-level habit stuff, but they're actually... they're kind of tied to everything else, aren't they? your budget, where you live, what's around you, what you grew up with. for me in newcastle, the cheap spots near work — they're usually doing meat. that's what's available and that's what i can afford. so it feels practical and automatic, but it's actually shaped by a lot of stuff underneath. i eat what nameref described basically — red meat maybe two, three times a week, chicken, bit of fish. and honestly i don't think about it much beyond whether it fits what i need on the day. but if someone was sitting here saying that doesn't matter, that it's all just habit or whatever, i'd push back on that. it matters because it's real, because it's what actually works for people's lives. not everything has to be this big conscious choice to be meaningful, you know?

items.speaker: S04
items.quote: yeah, for me it's pretty practical, to be honest. i mean, it's usually what's on offer near me or what i've already got in — i work in the city centre, so i'll often just grab something from one of the usual spots on my lunch break. there's a few places i rotate through, places i know do decent food that don't cost an arm and a leg. and then at home, it's a mix of what's in the fridge already and what i can't be bothered to cook, really. if i've got chicken or fish in there, that's an easy one — quick to sort out. i eat a fair bit of fish actually, couple times a week usually. red meat maybe once a week, depending. but yeah, it's not that deep for me — it's cost, it's what's available, it's what doesn't take forever to cook. habit too, i suppose. you end up doing the same things because they work, don't you? and convenience matters. like, if it's a tuesday night and i'm knackered, i'm not thinking about some big philosophical choice — i'm thinking about what takes twenty minutes and tastes alright. that's the real decision for most people, i reckon. not what you think you should eat, but what actually works with your life.

items.speaker: S02
items.quote: but that's the thing though — i don't think you're trapped either way, actually. like, i get what you're saying about the stress, but there's a difference between accepting you've got limited options and feeling like you're constantly making the wrong choice because an app's designed to make you doubt yourself. like, if there was just the chippy, yeah, you'd accept it. but that's not really the middle ground, is it? the middle ground would be... i dunno, knowing a few decent spots, having a rough idea of what they do, and just going there without spending twenty minutes second-guessing yourself on a screen. and i think that's what's actually changed. it's not the choice itself — it's that these apps, they're literally designed to keep you scrolling, looking at more options, reading reviews from random people you don't know. they want you to feel uncertain because that keeps you engaged. they're making money off you sitting there for ages going back and forth. whereas before, you'd maybe ask a mate, or you'd just know from experience that the chippy was alright, and you'd go. you weren't isolated with a phone making you feel like you're constantly wrong. i think the difference is... you can have genuine choice without all that anxiety built in. but the way these things work now, they're kind of weaponising the choice against you, if that makes sense. it's not about having options, it's about having options that are designed to stress you out.

items.speaker: S04
items.quote: no, fair point actually. i hadn't really thought about it that way. i mean, i've got options round here — there's loads of pubs within walking distance, so i can just pick one that feels right. but yeah, if you're somewhere more spread out and half of them have gone under or changed completely, that's... that's a different problem. and the driving thing makes sense. like, it's not really a local spot anymore if you've got to drive twenty minutes to get there, is it? you lose the whole casual thing about it. you can't just pop round the corner because you're bored. i suppose i'm a bit lucky that way. there's enough places near me that i can find somewhere that works without it being this big effort.

items.speaker: S03
items.quote: honestly? it feels shit, to be fair. like, there's a difference between understanding something intellectually and actually feeling it, you know? and sitting here saying it out loud, realizing that i'm kind of... colluding with the thing i'm complaining about — that's different to just thinking it to yourself. because when it's just in your head, you can kind of... rationalize it. you can go, well, the places are changing anyway, everyone's using apps, it's just how things are now. but saying it here, with you lot listening, it's harder to do that. and the mad thing is, i'm not even in nameref 's situation where there's actual solid consequences. like, i could probably just go out, order what i want, be visible in a space, and nothing particularly bad would happen. maybe someone would make a comment. maybe not. and i'm just... not testing that because it's easier not to. so there's this feeling of like... i'm wasting something, maybe? like, i've got options that nameref doesn't have, and i'm squandering them by just staying home. which sounds dramatic, but that's kind of what it feels like when you actually say it out loud. but also — and this is the other part that's getting to me — i'm not sure just feeling shit about it changes anything, does it? like, i could walk out of here today and decide i'm gonna go out more, use the actual spaces, stop hiding behind the app. but then next week when i'm tired, when it's easier to just order something, when there's no one else going out... i'll probably just do the same thing again. so it's like, knowing it feels a bit hollow. it doesn't actually move anything.

items.speaker: S04
items.quote: yeah, so for me it's probably the pub near where i live, actually. there's this one called the grapes down in the city centre — nothing fancy, just a proper local. we go there most weekends if we're not doing anything else. it's got decent beer, the staff know us by now, and you can actually hear each other talk, which sounds basic but you'd be surprised how many places you can't. i think the main thing is it's just... low-key, you know? no one's trying too hard. you can sit there for three hours nursing a couple of pints, chat about whatever — football, work drama, sometimes just mess about — and there's no pressure to be doing something else or going somewhere flashier. it's just a place where you can actually be.

items.speaker: S02
items.quote: uh, kind of just depends what we're all feeling, to be honest. like, i don't think we ever go out with like a set place in mind unless we've booked somewhere but like otherwise we're out for a few drinks it's like just decide what we want to eat and then there's loads of places around it so we just pick one after that.

items.speaker: S01
items.quote: i've been listening to what nameref and nameref have been saying, and that's... that matters, what they've said. but i'm sitting here thinking about something different, and i need to say it because i think i've been missing what's actually the problem. nameref 's lost his wife. nameref 's dealing with grief, with loss. that's real, that's hard. but i'm still here, my wife's still here, she's still making the meals, i'm still showing up at the table. and what i'm realizing is — i'm in a different trap than they are. because when i said earlier that i don't know how to cook, that i can't manage without her — i wasn't just talking about not having learned. i was talking about something i've never had to face. and maybe that's the actual problem. because as long as she's doing it, as long as i'm relying on her, i don't ever have to change. i don't ever have to decide what i actually believe about anything — food, what i deserve, what matters to me. i can just keep showing up at the table and accepting whatever happens. and that's different from what nameref went through. he had to learn, he had to rebuild it. but i'm choosing not to even try, not even think about it, because someone else is handling it. because i can get away with not knowing. so when you're asking what would make plant-based more appealing — i don't know if that's even the right question for me. because the real question is whether i'd ever actually decide anything for myself at all, or if i'm just going to keep living off the back of what my wife thinks is right. and that's harder to sit with than any of this other stuff, i think.

items.speaker: S03
items.quote: i hear what nameref 's saying, and i think he's right to push back on that. because i've been sitting here nodding along with nameref and nameref about the embedded thing, and it sounds good when you say it — people noticing, the infrastructure — but nameref 's naming something i haven't really wanted to admit. my mate steve, lived three streets over from me for fifteen years. we'd see each other all the time, proper embedded, knew his routines, his kids went to the same school as mine. his wife died suddenly about four years ago, and honestly? people were around for about two weeks. then they just... weren't. and he was still here, still on the same street, still going to the same pub. but he was lonely as anything. the routine just meant he was lonely in a familiar place. so i think nameref 's right that it's a foundation, or whatever — it's easier maybe. but nameref 's right too. knowing people and them actually being there when something matters are two different things. i'd got a bit carried away with painting it as this perfect safety thing, and it's not. it's just... it's where you are. it helps sometimes. doesn't guarantee anything.

items.speaker: S04
items.quote: yeah, i think i'm mostly where they are, but... i dunno, i'm not entirely sure i can say it as cleanly as that, to be honest. like, i do like eating meat. that's genuine — i'm not pretending i don't. but when i think about actually going plant-based, the thing that gets me is i can't quite tell what's me choosing it versus what's just... comfortable because it's what i know, you know? like, nameref said both things are true at the same time, and i think that's right. but i think for me the honest bit is — i'm not sure i fully know which is which. like, do i want meat because it's genuinely what i'd pick if everything was neutral? or do i want it because it's normal and easy and doesn't require me to think about anything or explain myself? and i reckon if i'm being straight, i don't really know the answer to that. it's probably both, but i can't untangle it from where i'm sitting. so yeah, the inertia is real, the comfort is real — but i'm also not gonna sit here and pretend i'm totally clear that i'd choose this anyway if things were set up differently. maybe i would, maybe i wouldn't. that's the honest answer. it just works fine as it is, so i'm not... doing the work to figure it out, i suppose.

items.speaker: S04
items.quote: i'm not actually sure anything could be done to make plant based foods more appealing to me because i've must have, i'm just thinking, like, whenever you go out for a sunday roast, or whatever, like 95% of your plate is plant based. it's just like the roast beef or the roast chicken, whatever it is, you have. like, i actually don't want to give that up full stop. there's potatoes, carrots, whatever else happens to be on that plate most of the time. but to me the mix is actually quite important. like i really want that versus the other stuff to be honest. so i don't think there is anything that's gonna make me switch. like the only thing that's gonna stop me from consuming meat, is if the government turn around and put the tax way up on it, and it becomes unaffordable. but even then it's going to be, i’m probably still going to do my best to go and get it anyway. so i guess the cost of meat is actually what would make plant based foods more appealing. but it’s gonna have to, it would have to become extortionately expensive for me to change.

items.speaker: S01
items.quote: yeah, i know what you mean about having the time to notice, nameref . that part's true for me as well. though i've gone a bit the other direction, if i'm honest. i eat meat maybe once a week, sometimes a bit more — chicken mostly, bit of fish now and then. red meat not very often. but it's not because i've decided against it or anything. it's just what makes sense when you're actually thinking about it instead of just... i dunno, defaulting to something. i'll have chicken one night, then eggs another night, bit of dairy, veg — it's just what works. don't need meat every day or anything. but it's like you said — you've got time now to actually look at what you're buying instead of just grabbing the same old thing. for me that meant realizing i don't particularly need meat three times a week or whatever. doesn't mean i don't eat it. i do. it's just... it's a regular part of what i eat, but not the centerpiece of everything, if that makes sense. not because i've got some strong feeling about it either way. just what seems reasonable when you actually think about it.

items.speaker: S03
items.quote: that's the thing though, nameref . you don't spend time thinking about it because you don't have to. you've never had to question it. it just feels natural because it's what everyone around you does, what you've always done. but that doesn't mean it's what you actually want — it just means you can't tell the difference anymore. i think about it because i've got no choice. if i wanted something different, i'd have to face it head on. but you — you can just drift with it and call it preference because there's no friction. no one's saying anything to you about it, so it feels like your choice. but if you walked into the pub tomorrow and ordered a salad, you'd notice something, wouldn't you? you'd feel it. and that feeling — that's not nothing. that's the pressure doing its work even when no one's said a word.

items.speaker: S01
items.quote: fair point, yeah. i didn't mean it to sound like you lot are doing it wrong or anything. i get it — when things are spread out more, you need to actually nail down when you're seeing each other, or you just won't. that makes sense. and you're right, it does mean you end up seeing your mates more often if you're actually planning it properly rather than just hoping it'll happen. i suppose it's just... i don't know, different approach depending on where you are and what your life looks like. round here with the pubs closing, we're probably heading that way whether we like it or not — might have to start doing the organised thing more ourselves. can't rely on just knowing where everyone's going to be if there's nowhere left to go, can you. but yeah, you're not wrong about that community side of it either. i was maybe thinking too much about the anonymity bit — that's more about not having people in your business on a daily basis, but the actual pub, knowing who's in there, bumping into someone and having a chat — that's different. that's the good kind of knowing people, if you know what i mean. lose that and you do lose something.

items.speaker: S01
items.quote: right, but that's not quite what i'm saying, nameref . i'm not saying you have to do anything — you're right, you could live anywhere and stick with what you know. but i'm talking about friction, aren't i? in a village, if you want a curry, you probably have to plan it, maybe travel somewhere, maybe it's not even that good when you get there. so you don't bother as much. in manchester, you walk out your door and there's a decent curry place on the corner. your mate says let's grab thai — it's five minutes away. you're not making some big conscious decision each time. it's just easier, so you end up doing it more. that's not about me being indecisive or you being stubborn — it's just how friction works, innit? and yeah, we've probably got similar takeaways available to you lot round here too, but the difference is density and quality. if there's only one dodgy chinese place within twenty minutes, you're not going to bother much. if there's five restaurants and they're all decent, you will. that's not a personal choice thing — that's just how it plays out. i'm not saying the place determines what you do. i'm saying it makes certain paths easier than others. you can still choose differently, but most people don't when they don't have to.

items.speaker: S05
items.quote: yeah, it's a bit different for me though, i reckon. like, you've got the habit side of it — i eat meat regularly, dairy most days, that's just what i do. but where i am, there's also the practical bit, you know? you can't just think about what you fancy and expect to get it. if i want decent meat, i'm likely getting it from the local butcher or the farm shop, or there's one supermarket maybe twenty minutes away. so it's not as casual as just coming home and deciding. you kind of plan around what's actually available, what you can actually get to. and the dairy stuff — milk, cheese, whatever — that's more built in because those are the things you can reliably get anywhere. it's less of a choice and more just... this is what's here. so i guess i'm saying the habit part makes sense, but for me there's also just the constraint of living somewhere rural. you're not overthinking it philosophically or anything, but you're definitely more aware of where your food's coming from and what your options actually are. it's more intentional by default, if that makes sense.

items.speaker: S01
items.quote: for me it's pretty straightforward, really. i eat meat most days — couple times a week red meat, couple times poultry. i'll have fish maybe once a month or so. and eggs pretty much every day, dairy as well. honestly, it's just what i've always done. i don't think about it that much. it's convenient, it's what i grew up eating, and i enjoy it. i'll have a curry, a steak, some chicken — it's just normal to me. i'm not like... militant about it or anything. i just eat what i fancy and what's available. that's sort of it.

items.speaker: S02
items.quote: yeah, that makes sense. that's a different thing entirely, isn't it — when you can't actually just be anonymous. i hadn't really thought about it that way, but you're right. in the city you've got that luxury where you can walk into a pub and nobody's clocking who you are or reporting back to anyone. you're just... there. i think that does change things. like, when nameref says being seen being normal — that's a pressure, isn't it? even if it sounds like a small thing. because then you're managing how you come across the whole time. whereas in the pub round mine, you can just be a bit messy, a bit loud, whatever. nobody cares because it's not a statement about anything. it's just what you're doing that night. i'd probably go a bit mad if i had to be that conscious about it every time i went out with mates. fair play for dealing with that, honestly.

items.speaker: S03
items.quote: right, well... that's interesting, nameref , because hearing you say that, i'm not sure i entirely believe it for myself, to be honest. i mean, i hear what you're saying — that it loosens up, that you can change it. and fair play to you for doing that. but i've been eating the same way for over seventy years now. it's not just a habit, is it? it's... it's who i am, sort of. the way i think about food, about what's proper to eat. and i know that sounds daft when you put it like that, but it's different when it's actually you living it. i mean, i can see intellectually that you've shifted yours, that you feel better for it. and maybe that's brilliant for you. but i look at myself and i think, i'm not going to change that now. i don't want to. it feels... i don't know, it feels like giving up something that matters, even if i can't quite explain why. though... i suppose hearing you say it's possible, that it's not just stuck there forever, that does something. it's not that i think i will change — i don't reckon i will. but it's different hearing someone say it loosens up, rather than just accepting it as fixed. makes me wonder if i'm just being stubborn about it, or if there's actually something there. i don't know. bit of both, probably. but yeah, what you said — it's landed with me a bit.

items.speaker: S02
items.quote: right, so i think there's a practical answer and then there's the other bit. practically — and i've seen this — it's about food that actually satisfies you, isn't it? plant-based stuff that's hearty, that fills you up. a lot of the stuff marketed at blokes is either trying too hard to be meat — like, a fake burger that's trying to taste exactly like beef — or it's the opposite, it's all kale and quinoa bowls. neither of those works for most lads i know. but the stuff that does work — a proper lentil stew, bean chilli, that kind of thing — people eat it without thinking about whether it's plant-based or not. they're just eating food that tastes good and sticks with them. i know blokes who eat that regularly and don't make a fuss about it. the real problem though — and this is what you can't solve just by making better food — is the whole thing around it. if plant-based became just... normal, if there wasn't this edge to it, this idea that it means something about you as a man, then it'd probably shift. but that's the part that's actually hard. because like, we've been talking about all this social pressure, the comments, the invisibility of the default. you could have the best plant-based food in the world, but if the moment you order it you're braced for the "oh, gone soft have we" comments, most blokes aren't going to bother. it's not worth the hassle. so i reckon what would actually change things is if people — blokes especially — just... stopped making it weird. stopped the comments, stopped treating it like it means something. that sounds simple, but it's actually the hard bit, isn't it?

items.speaker: S03
items.quote: yeah, there's a couple of spots i go back to regularly, actually. there's this pub not far from me — been going there for years now. it's nothing fancy, right, but that's sort of the point. you get the same faces most weekends, people you've known for ages, and the staff know what you drink. you can sit there and actually have a proper conversation without feeling like you need to order something every five minutes or like you're taking up space. there's a kind of... i dunno, an understanding there. you're not performing, if that makes sense. you're just having a chat with people you know. the atmosphere's relaxed. it's not trying to be trendy or anything — it's just a working men's pub really, but that's what makes it work. everyone's in the same boat, you know? similar age, similar lives, kids, work stress, all that stuff. and then there's a cafe i'll pop into now and then during the day, bit more casual than the pub, but again it's the regulars thing. you see the same owner, same other people coming in, and there's just this kind of rhythm to it. you're not rushed. that matters, i think — you've got time to actually sit and talk rather than feeling like you need to get somewhere.

items.speaker: S04
items.quote: yeah, plant based. i think mostly plant based are vegetables. i don't know. yeah, i bet it was. i read that back there in nigeria. uh, some vegetables like that, uh, mostly, you know, they are plant based and they are good for the body, very good for the body, uh, uh, good for the heart, uh, and it makes you, it makes you, uh, it makes you watch your body very well, and they are good for with, uh, uh, for checking of your weight also mostly.

items.speaker: S01
items.quote: maybe i can start like for eating if i go for, maybe let's say wetherspoon or somewhere, i firstly check the menu actually if i like something. um, for me, i don't eat pork. that's why like this is my limitations and other options i just check in what i can eat. in that day if i feel for example want to eat meat or like beef or chicken depends on that i choose but generally choose chicken i think i'd like that.

items.speaker: S04
items.quote: yeah. nameref 's put his finger on it, hasn't he. that's the thing that's been nagging at me too, if i'm honest. because i've been telling myself for years — right, i'm just eating sensibly, i'm not making some big statement about it, i'm just choosing what makes sense practically. and i still think that's true, in a way. but nameref 's right — once you're actually living it, once people know about it, once it's visible... it becomes a position whether you want it to or not. i can't just eat fish and eggs and veg and pretend nobody's noticing or thinking about it. they are. and the more i do it, the more it sticks — i'm the bloke in the village who eats differently. that's what i am now, whether i wanted to be or not. and i hate that. i hate that i can't just make a practical choice about what i eat without it meaning something bigger. but nameref 's saying the truth of it — you can't slip sideways into living differently and stay invisible. once you're actually doing it, it's a thing. it's a position. so the bit that gets under my skin is... i didn't want this to be who i am. i just wanted to eat sensibly and not have it turn into some statement about me. but it has. and i can't undo that in the village i live in. everyone already knows. i'm already that person.

items.speaker: S02
items.quote: yeah, honestly? by the end of a long commute day, it's just... whatever requires the least thinking, really. i mean, i'll come home knackered from getting the train back, and my wife's usually got the kids sorted or doing homework or something, and the last thing either of us has got energy for is standing in the kitchen trying to figure out what we're going to cook. so a lot of the time it's just — what's easy? pasta, beans on toast, something we can throw together in twenty minutes. or if it's been a particularly bad day with the trains, we'll just order a takeaway because you're too tired to even do that. and then you feel a bit guilty about it, but you know what, you've had a shit day and you need to just get food in people. it's not like we sit down and think, right, we need a balanced meal. it's more like — what can we physically do given that we're all wrecked? the decision-making's already exhausted by the time you get home, if i'm honest. you've had to make decisions all day, deal with delays, figure out plans that didn't work out, and then you come back and you've just got no bandwidth left for it. my wife and i have definitely said that to each other — on the days when the commute's been fine, we're a bit more inclined to actually cook something. so yeah, it does all link up, doesn't it.

items.speaker: S03
items.quote: exactly, yeah. that's two different problems. and i think what nameref 's saying there is spot on — you've got to get past the first barrier before you even get to test whether the second one matters. i went to this place a few months back, right, with some mates. and they had this vegan option that was actually... it looked decent, you know? not all fancy with flowers or whatever. just a solid-looking wrap with some good stuff in it. and i thought, fair enough, i'll give it a go. and it was genuinely decent — better than i expected, to be honest. proper filling, nice flavors, didn't feel like i was compromising. and that's the thing — once i'd actually tried it and it was alright, the whole signalling thing kind of fell away. because it wasn't about making a statement, it was just about getting something decent to eat. and i'd probably order it again if i was there. but that only happened because the first barrier — the presentation, the way it was framed — wasn't too heavy. if it had been all fancy and artisanal or whatever, i probably wouldn't have ordered it in the first place. so you need both things working.

items.speaker: S03
items.quote: yeah, okay, that's fair. you're right — context matters, and i was maybe oversimplifying it a bit. but i think i've been conflating two different things without really sitting with where the actual tension is. like, there's the pressure from new people or bigger groups — that's real, that's external pressure. but then there's also the stuff i do to myself even with my regular lads, and those aren't quite the same thing, are they? like, i said i've ordered a salad with no problem, but if i'm honest, there's still times when i don't. and i'm not always sure if that's because i actually think someone'll judge me or because i'm just... used to not doing it. it's become automatic. that's different from walking into a room full of people you don't know and thinking "i better order a burger so i don't look soft." the thing is, if you don't actually test that assumption with your regular mates — if you just keep performing the same way because you've always done it — you don't really know if it's them or you, do you? and that matters because it affects what you can actually change. with nameref 's point about new groups or bigger setups, yeah, that's harder. you're genuinely more exposed. but with your actual mates, your core people — i reckon there's something worth trying to shift there. otherwise you're just... forever managing an image that maybe doesn't even need managing anymore.

items.speaker: S05
items.quote: nah, i don't think it's quite that different though, nameref . like, i get what you're saying — you've got the options there — but it's not just about whether you can be bothered, is it? it's more complicated than that. because yeah, there's only one shop out here, but it's not like i'm sat at home thinking "i could drive twenty minutes to the next town if i really wanted to." that's just not realistic for a weeknight when you're knackered after work. so there's a constraint there, but it's not just... one shop exists. it's the whole thing — the distance, the time, the hassle of it. and you saying it's on you because you've got options everywhere... i don't know, man. like, yeah, there's loads of places, but you still need to actually know what you want, go there, figure it out. that's effort too, just a different kind. you're comparing yourself to a version of you that goes exploring different takeaways or shops all the time, but that's not really how anyone lives, is it? i think the defaulting thing is just... normal. whether it's because there's literally nothing else or because trying something new requires more effort than just getting what you know — the end result's pretty similar. you're not choosing, you're just doing what's easiest. it's not a failure thing necessarily.

items.speaker: S02
items.quote: yeah, well it's a bit different where i am. i mean, i'm suburban, so i've got options, haven't i. there's pubs within walking distance, a couple of them. i'll meet mates down the local — it's just round the corner basically, five minutes walk. that's the main one for us. we just sort of... go when we fancy it, really. don't have to plan it too much. but what you're saying about the intention thing, nameref — i get that, i do. out where you are you've got to make more of an effort. we're a bit spoiled, i suppose. we can just say, oh, fancy a pint, and off we go. though i will say, even in the suburbs you do end up at someone's house quite a bit. my mate dave, he's always got something on the go — bit of diy, garden work, that sort of thing. i'll pop over, we'll have a cup of tea, help him out with whatever it is. that's the same as what you're describing, nameref . you're doing something and chatting at the same time. that's quite nice, actually. more relaxed than just sitting making small talk. but yeah, the difference is we've got the pub right there if we want it. we can be a bit more casual about it. not everything has to be an event.

items.speaker: S03
items.quote: right, okay — yeah, that's cleaner, and i respect that you're being straight about it. but i think there's maybe still something underneath that that's worth just... noticing, you know? because when you say "i just don't want it," that feels clear from where you're sitting. but i'm not sure you can actually know what wanting feels like separate from what's been normal your whole life. like, you've eaten meat your whole life, everyone around you eats meat, it's just what's there — so of course you don't want something else. that's not the same as saying you'd definitely still not want it if things had been different from the start. and i don't mean that in a way that's trying to prove you're being controlled or whatever — i'm not saying that. i'm just saying... there's a difference between "i don't want plant-based food" and "i can't really imagine wanting plant-based food because it's never been normalized around me the way meat has." and i think for a lot of us, especially up here, it's closer to the second thing than the first. like, that's what i was getting at before about newcastle and what's embedded. it's not about you being weak or not thinking for yourself — it's just that wanting itself gets shaped by what you grow up around. so when you say you don't want it, yeah, that's probably true. but i'm not sure you can fully separate that from the fact that you've only ever really had the one thing normalized in the first place. that's the bit i think matters to just sit with, rather than moving past it to "okay so i just don't want it, done." does that make sense?

items.speaker: S04
items.quote: i think it does, actually. not in how nameref was describing — not in some big statement way. but out here in the village, there's definitely... there's an expectation, still, isn't there. that men eat meat. that's what a man does. you go down the pub, you order a steak or a pie with meat in it, and that's just what you do. i've noticed it more since i've retired, funnily enough. when you were working, nobody was really watching what you had for lunch. but when you're more visible in the community, doing your shopping, chatting to people — there's this quiet thing where meat's still tied up with... being a proper man, still, even now. it's not people saying it outright usually. it's more in the little comments, the assumptions about what you'd want. i eat meat, right. couple times a week, fish, eggs, dairy — it all works fine. but i've definitely felt that pressure, especially when i was eating less regularly for a bit. you'd mention it to someone and there'd be this... look. like you'd gone soft or something. which is daft, but it's there. the thing that bothers me about it, if i'm honest, is not the eating meat or not eating meat — that's fine either way. it's that the assumption's still so strong. like, you can't just make a reasonable choice about what makes sense for you without it meaning something about whether you're masculine or not. that's the bit that feels outdated to me. you should just be able to eat what you want without all that baggage attached to it.

items.speaker: S02
items.quote: i'd actually push back a bit on how nameref 's framing that, to be honest. because i don't think it's just about the routine getting stale or whatever — like, yeah, that happens, but i think there's a difference between that and what i'd say i'm actually doing. like, i'm not sitting at someone's yard thinking "oh god, i'm bored, i need to mix it up." it's more that i'm actively choosing to do different stuff because i want to, you know? i'll go out with mates, i'll do something solo, i'll try a new place — not because the old thing got boring or i'm running away from routine, but because i actually want to do those things. it's kind of a different headspace. i think what nameref 's saying has got a point too — there's nothing wrong with just being happy where you are. but for me it's less about comfort having a shelf life and more about just... naturally wanting to try stuff. going to a gig, meeting someone new, checking out a different area of glasgow, whatever. that's just what i'm into at the moment. so i don't know if it's as straightforward as "you'll get bored of the yard and need to branch out." might be more that as you get older you want different things, not just different for the sake of it.

items.speaker: S03
items.quote: yeah, i know exactly what you mean, nameref . i've felt it. not constantly, but yeah — you mention you're having fish instead, or you're doing a bit more veg, and there's that moment where someone just... they clock it. and there's this little edge to the response, like you've said something slightly odd. the frustrating bit for me is that it's so quiet, isn't it. nobody's saying anything outright. but you feel it. and that's the noise i was talking about — not necessarily people being preachy about what they eat, but this whole thing where eating meat gets tangled up with being a man, still, in 2024 or whenever we are now. it feels... i don't know, embarrassing almost, that it's still like that. because you're right — you should just be able to say, oh i'm having eggs tonight, or fish, and nobody blinks. it shouldn't mean anything about you. but it does seem to, in people's heads. i've noticed it too, down here in the suburbs. maybe less intense than out in a village like you've got, but it's there. that little assumption that if you're not eating meat you're somehow... less something. and that's what gets my back up, i think. not the eating or not eating. just that the whole thing's still loaded with all this baggage that doesn't need to be there.

items.speaker: S03
items.quote: yeah, i mean... i'm kind of in between what you two are saying, i reckon. like, i've got enough places round here in the north east — i'm not as bad off as nameref makes it sound — but it's definitely changing. there's definitely pubs i used to go to that have shut down or turned into something else. the thing is though, round where i am, it's not just about them closing. it's more like... they're spreading out, you know? so you've got your city centre spots, fair enough, loads of choice there. but then between that and where people actually live, it's getting thinner. used to be there was a decent pub or two you could walk to from most places, and now you're either in town or you're not really going anywhere casual. so it's not quite as bad as what nameref 's describing where you've got to drive twenty minutes, but it's getting there. and i think that does change things. like, me and my mates, we still go out pretty regular, but we're going into town more often than we used to. which is fine, but it's less of a... i dunno, a neighbourhood thing. you're not bumping into your mates by accident like you might have done if there was something local. and the messaging thing nameref mentioned — yeah, that tracks. you message more because you're not just seeing people naturally. so it becomes more... arranged, like nameref said.

items.speaker: S05
items.quote: i think nameref 's right that you can't fully separate wanting from what's been normalized, but i also think he might be missing something about how complete it is out where i am, you know? like, nameref 's saying "if it was as easy as meat," but the thing is — where i live, there basically isn't an alternative to notice in the first place. it's not like the infrastructure's there but you have to seek it out. it's just... not there. you go to the local shop, you get meat. you go to the chippy, you get meat. you're at someone's house, there's meat. there's no moment where you go "oh, i could have something else instead" because there isn't something else. so i don't know if ease is even the right way to think about it for me. it's more like — the thing just doesn't exist in your world, so you can't really want it because you're not even aware it's an option most days. i suppose if there was actually a plant-based option available somewhere near me — properly available, not like a special trip to somewhere twenty minutes away — then maybe i'd notice it more, think about it more. maybe i'd try it occasionally just because it was there. but that's different from shifting what i actually want to eat regularly, you know? that would require something beyond just availability. it would require... i dunno, a reason to care enough to change, and i don't have one. so yeah, availability matters, but not in the way nameref was talking about. it's not about ease making something appealing. it's more that without any visibility of an alternative, you can't even get to the point of having a choice to make.

items.speaker: S04
items.quote: i don't really think gender comes into it massively for me as a conscious thought, but like the minute we started getting a bit of summer and a bit of sun. um, i had this idea in my head that i really want to get into offset smoking. um, which if anyone doesn't know, it's like where you do like, you smoke like meat. so you put like a rack of ribs on like a barbecue and then you've got the, the thick heat there and the, the, it comes through and i was explaining all this stuff to my fiance and i was going on about it and she was just looking at me like, could we not just grill something, like, that'll take 20 minutes? why are you talking about smoking ribs for seven hours? and i was like going, but i've got this really cool toy and i've just bought a chimney for the, for the, for the charcoal and all this stuff that i was going through. i could see she'd be really happy to eat the food at the end of it, but she did not share my enthusiasm for standing over a hot fire. i'm playing a bit and i suppose on a, on a sort of a cliched gender conversation, bloke playing with a barbecue or standing there has a, has a kind of cultural perception that you kind of go, we like doing that. um, and i do enjoy it, but that's because i generally, i enjoy the process of cooking the food, i enjoy serving the food and i enjoy the flavour that i'm creating with it. um, but it, it, it doesn't, it doesn't hit me as being a, a blokey thing. although the only people i speak to about it that also engage with that and in the process, are all of the blokes that do it. you know, i've got a few mates who have got, who got me into it. um, i've got female friends. not one of them has any interest in the process. they're very interested in the eating of it. and they, they, they like the, the cuisine and the idea of what you're doing. but they, they don't share the same enthusiasm as when you get, you know, a meat thermometer delivered or, you know, butchers paper and all this stuff that you buy to go along with it. um, you, i get very excited about it, but they don't. um, so i don't know if that's necessarily, that's not my gender influencing me in that manner. to eat that stuff, i think i'd eat that no matter what because it tastes good. but the preparation side of it, i do feel there's quite a cliched masculinity about it.

items.speaker: S02
items.quote: yeah, look — i think i need to be a bit honest here. because i was sort of implying earlier that i'm quite deliberate about where i shop and all that, but the truth is most of my day-to-day eating is just... easy, isn't it? habit. i'll grab what's convenient, what's in the cupboard, what i know my family will eat without complaint. the pub thing, yeah, i notice the quality there because you're sitting down, you've got time, you're paying attention. someone's put effort in, it's a bit of an occasion. but at home? i'm probably throwing together a bit of chicken, some veg, done in twenty minutes because that's what fits around everything else. i'm not thinking about where the chicken came from or whether it's been looked after properly — i'm thinking about whether the kids will eat it and whether i can get it on the table before we're all hangry. so when i pushed back about having good local options, that's true — they are there. but i'm not actually using them as much as i maybe made it sound. it's more just... they exist if i can be bothered, which most nights i'm not. most of the time it's just whatever's easiest.

items.speaker: S01
items.quote: yeah, but i think in the city it's kind of a different thing altogether, innit. like, i've got loads of places round birmingham — probably too many, honestly. there's bars, pubs, cafes, whatever. but that's almost the problem sometimes. like, you lot are talking about things shutting down and having to drive somewhere, and fair enough that's rough. but round here it's more like... everything's still there, right, but it's either a wetherspoons or some fancy cocktail place, or it's in broad street where it costs you thirty quid before you've even sat down. or it's got this whole vibe attached to it — you know what i mean? it's not just a place you go, it's a thing. and then you've got these pockets where certain groups go, so you kind of know which places are which. like, you wouldn't necessarily bump into your mates by accident because everyone's spread across different areas depending on... i dunno, where you're from, what your thing is. it's not like there's one local spot where everyone in your neighbourhood naturally ends up. i get what you're saying about messaging more and it being more arranged though — that's definitely true here as well. you message and you plan which bar, which area, whatever. but there's loads of choice, so it's almost harder to just... be somewhere casual, if that makes sense. you're always aware you could be somewhere else, somewhere supposedly better.

items.speaker: S03
items.quote: yeah, that's... that's actually hit on something i've been thinking about while you lot have been talking. because you're right, nameref — out here in the suburbs we've got all these options now. there's pubs, cafes, restaurants, you name it. i can drive ten minutes and have a choice of where to go. used to be you'd just go to your local, the one near home, and that was it. everyone went there, you saw the same faces. but now? now i can go anywhere i fancy, and so can everyone else. which sounds like a good thing, doesn't it? but what you're describing — knowing the landlord, bumping into people you know — that's actually something i've lost without really noticing it happening. i can go to a different pub every week if i want, but i don't know anyone there. no one knows me. and the funny thing is, nameref , you're saying you've got limited options and you work with what you've got. but at least with that — at least everyone in the village ends up at the same pub sometimes, right? so you actually build something. you actually know people. whereas i've got all these choices and i don't feel like i've got much of a community anymore. the old local i used to go to, it's not even there anymore — it's a wine bar or something now, different crowd entirely. so sometimes i think, what's the point of having all these options if you lose the connection that comes with just... doing the same thing, going to the same place, seeing the same people?

items.speaker: S04
items.quote: yeah. like you're not going to replicate a really good burger or a really good steak. so actually, you know, maybe an aubergine parmesan, like i'd never had that before. and i thought that's really good. you know, i really enjoyed it. it's something that i couldn't imagine having, um, obviously didn't use vegan or plant based cheese, but you know, it's like something that's so not a meat dish. i was like, okay, yeah, you know, i actually, i wouldn't cook it every night, but i could eat it once a week or something, you know, go, go, go hard in the other direction, i think, and actually own it. [ nameref : yeah.] that's, that's how i, that's what it’d do to me. but really, is anything really going to make it appealing to me, not majorly.

items.speaker: S02
items.quote: no, but that awareness you just described — that's the thing, innit? you said it yourself. you went down the pub, had a steak, and you were aware it could be read a certain way. that awareness didn't come from nowhere. that's you responding to the shift. that's not external anymore, that's in your head now. i'm not saying you created it or you're doing anything wrong. but the fact that you're *aware* of how it could be read — that means the shift isn't just something happening to you from the outside. you're part of how it's working now. you're thinking about it differently, even if you're not changing what you eat. that's what i mean about it going both ways. it's not like there's some external force making you self-conscious about having a steak, and then there's you, just innocently eating. the self-consciousness is part of how the whole thing's moving. you can't have the awareness without being part of the shift, even if you're not deliberately making a point about it. i don't think that's a criticism of you, by the way. i'm just saying — the idea that this is all happening to us, externally, and we're just passively having it done to us? that's not quite how it works. we're in it. the awareness itself is part of it.

items.speaker: S03
items.quote: that's fair, yeah. maybe it's not just about age then. like, i said i don't care anymore, but that's probably because i've known the same lads for years, you know? so it's not even a thing. but if i was going out with work people i didn't know well, or someone new's joined the group, i might still do it without even realizing. you're right about that — context matters more than just how old you are. it's a bit like what you said though, about not really thinking about it enough to challenge it. like, once you get comfortable in a situation, you stop noticing you're doing it. so it's not that i've gone, "right, i'm older now, i'm going to order what i want." it's more that the situation's just... easy. low stakes. no one's judging because we all know each other properly. but i reckon if you put me somewhere unfamiliar with new faces, i'd probably slip back into that a bit, without thinking. you'd just go for the safe option again, wouldn't you?

items.speaker: S04
items.quote: i mean... yeah, some of it does, actually. i wasn't going to say much because i've been fairly quiet while you lot have been working through all this, but nameref 's just said something that — yeah, it rings true. we did try to change things a bit with my wife, not long ago. nothing massive, but there was stuff we both said we wanted to do differently. and we kind of... we tried for a bit and then it just fell away. and the thing is, we didn't really talk about why it fell away. we just kind of accepted it didn't work and moved on. but what nameref 's saying — about having to know something different about yourself — that's closer to what actually happened, i think. because it wasn't that it was impossible. it was more that... we tried and it was harder than we expected, and we just kind of gave up. and then we didn't really look at why we gave up. we just accepted it. and the bit i'm recognizing now is — i don't know if we gave up because it was actually too hard, or because we didn't care enough to push through the hard bit. and if i'm being honest, i'm not sure i want to know the answer to that question about myself, or about us. because if we tried properly and it still fell apart, then yeah, what nameref said — it's not about circumstances anymore. it's about what we actually want, what we're actually willing to do. and that's a different thing to sit with than just going, oh well, we're both tired, it didn't work out.

items.speaker: S04
items.quote: yeah, i think the difference is when you do an asda shop or whatever, and you're looking at two baskets of food on the floor, but, you know, that used to be what you'd carry around in like a, you know, in your hands, um, and then, you know, now like 70 quid doesn't go very far. whereas, you know, when i, you know, first like, you know, 15 years ago, i know it's a long time ago, but like 70 quid felt like that was what, you know, a family of four, that was the weekly shop. now, like, you know, one person for a week, you know, 70 quid’s barely touching the sides. that's just getting, you know, your food. um, you know, when you factor in something like, you know, if you've got like a, you know, a young child, you need nappies, you know, or any cleaning products. all of a sudden a weekly shop is about 120, 150 quid just for the essentials. the plant based option, if it was bringing that down by a third would, would i think be appealing to a lot of people. um, you know, i think actually in some ways because it's more niche, it's costing more.

items.speaker: S03
items.quote: yeah, but i think nameref and nameref are treating that like it's a dead end, and i don't think it is. because here's the thing — the self-interested reason might actually be there already. it's just not about health or energy or whatever they're imagining. it's something different. like, for me, what actually shifted things wasn't someone telling me plant-based was good for me physically or for the planet. it was realizing i was just... accepting whatever the default was. going to the pub, ordering a burger because that's what you do. eating what my mum cooked without thinking about it. and at some point i noticed i was just doing what was easiest, what required no thought, what didn't make waves. and that felt shit, actually. not because of the food — because i wasn't making any choices at all. i was just defaulting into whatever took the least friction. so the self-interested reason isn't "i'll feel better or have more energy." it's autonomy. it's not being trapped by what's easy or what people expect. it's going "actually, i want to decide what i'm eating, not just accept what shows up in front of me." and that's personal. that's about me, not about the world. that's about not wanting to be the person who just goes along with things because thinking about it feels like too much bother. nameref 's saying there's no hook that's about him wanting to do it. but i reckon the hook might be there if he sat with what it actually feels like to just be on autopilot about everything. because that's not freedom, is it? that's just... letting life happen to you.

items.speaker: S05
items.quote: yeah, i get that — it's quick and straightforward. but i'd probably say for me it's a bit more of a choice, even if it doesn't feel like much of one, you know? like, at work i'll pack a sandwich with meat in it, or i'll grab a chicken wrap or whatever, and i'm kind of... i'm picking that. it's not like i'm not thinking about it. it's just a fast thought, not a long one. same at home — i'll have red meat maybe once a week, chicken a couple times a week. it's what i cook, it's what i know how to do, it works. but i'm still sort of... deciding on it, even if it's automatic. does that make sense? it's a decision i make without really deliberating, but i'm aware i'm making it, if that's the difference. i think it just depends what you mean by "decision," doesn't it? if you mean sitting down and weighing everything up, then yeah, that's not happening — but if you mean you're actually choosing something, then... i reckon most of us are, we're just doing it quickly without much fuss. like, i could have something different, but i'm picking meat because it's what i want and it's easy. that's still a choice, just not a complicated one.

items.speaker: S02
items.quote: tom kerridge, bloody hell. he's all money in the pocket, isn't he? you know? about 85 quid for steak and chips. you know what i mean? come on.

items.speaker: S02
items.quote: yeah, um, for me, one big thing is like, um, like the brands or whoever needs to accept that it’s a different kind of meal, meals, sorry, and, uh, not trying to pretend to be like what you avoid, like, cheese. like it's not cheese, but just give it another name. i don't, i don't have an example. but just to accept it. um, because i don't want to, it makes me feel like, like i'm, i'm lying to myself, pretending oh, i'm eating something that tastes like milk. but it’s not milk. you know, like. so yeah, just to be like to accept it is a different type of food, and they are different type of food and we already accept it. but that should be another one here. and it’s all fine. and, um, i'm sure more people will be interested eventually.

items.speaker: S02
items.quote: i think... honestly, i don't think i'd go fully plant-based. that's the thing. not because of what people think, and not really because of the social awkwardness bit, though nameref 's right that it's real in small places. it's more that i just don't see the reason for it, for me. like, i eat meat maybe once a month now. i eat fish, eggs, dairy — it all works fine. i'm not attached to any of it, but i'm also not... i dunno, i'm not trying to prove anything by cutting it all out completely. it just seems unnecessary, doesn't it. i've found a way of eating that makes sense to me and i'm fine with it. why would i change it again? nameref 's right about the habit thing too. i've got my rhythm now — it's not like i had to learn a whole new set of meals because i wasn't eating meat three times a week. i just eat differently. but going fully plant-based, that's a different thing. that's making a choice about something, in a bigger way. and there is a social bit to it, yeah. not in my village like nameref 's got — we're suburbs, people mind their own business more. but you do get... i suppose you become the bloke who's made that choice, and people notice it. not constantly, but they notice. and i'm not sure i want to be that visible about something that doesn't feel that important to me. the thing that bothers me more, if i'm honest, is when i see people pushing the idea that you should be doing it. that's when it gets to me — not the eating differently quietly, but the... the sense that there's something wrong if you're not. that there's some threat in it. that's what gets my back up.

items.speaker: S01
items.quote: right, well for me it's got to be the pub, hasn't it. i mean, i've got a couple of regulars i go to in manchester with the lads — we've been going to the same places for years now. there's just something about it, you know? you can talk, have a laugh, nobody's rushing you on. it's where we actually catch up properly. i work during the week, some of the lads are scattered about, so the pub's just... it's the place where we all naturally end up. you sit down with a pint, nobody's checking their phone every five seconds, or at least not as much, and you can have a proper conversation. or just sit in comfortable silence sometimes, which sounds daft but it's actually nice. i've tried the whole going to the cinema or whatever with mates, but it's not the same — you're sat there not talking for two hours. with the pub you've got that flexibility. you can stay for one and leave, or you can be there all night if it's a good night. it feels... i don't know, normal? like that's just what we do.

items.speaker: S01
