items.quote: yeah, i know exactly what you mean about the visibility thing. rural's rural, isn't it — everybody knows what everybody else is doing. so there's definitely that pressure there, that sense of being watched, even if nobody's saying anything outright. but i'll be honest — i haven't felt it as much as what you're describing, nameref . maybe i'm just not paying as much attention, or maybe it's different up here, but when i've mentioned eating fish or eggs or whatever, i haven't got that same sense of people clocking it like i've done something odd. could be that folk are a bit more live-and-let-live about it, or could be i'm just not as tuned into it. hard to say. what does get my back up though — and maybe this is what nameref was getting at earlier with the noise — is the whole idea that there's some kind of threat in it. like, if men aren't eating meat three times a week anymore, something's gone wrong. that feels daft to me. there's nothing threatening about choosing what makes sense for you to eat. that's just... being an adult and thinking about it, isn't it. the embarrassing bit for me is when people act like vegetarianism or eating less meat is somehow, i dunno, some kind of cultural thing that needs defending against. it's just food. people eat different things. that's always been true. i don't see why it's become this whole thing where you've got to pick a side and make a statement about it. but the village watching thing — yeah, i get that. that's real enough.

items.speaker: S01
items.quote: yeah, so for me it's kind of similar to what nameref said with the pub thing, to be honest. there's a few spots in birmingham we just tend to end up in — nothing fancy, just places where you know people and the vibe's alright. one of my mates works at a place in moseley, so we'll grab a drink there sometimes, but mostly it's just wherever feels right on the night, you know? could be someone's gaff, could be out somewhere. i think the thing nameref was saying about being able to actually talk — that resonates more than the specific place does, if that makes sense. like, i'm not massively fussed about whether it's indoors or outdoors or whatever. it's just... you want to be somewhere you can actually have a conversation without it being awkward or too loud or whatever. birmingham's busy enough that you've got options, but i don't think i'd say one thing beats the other necessarily. summer's obviously nicer for being outside, but winter you just find somewhere with a roof and get on with it. doesn't really bother me either way.

items.speaker: S01
items.quote: right, but see, that's the thing though — being casual about it isn't necessarily better, is it? i mean, you can pop down the pub whenever you fancy, but does that mean you see people deeper, you know what i mean? when you have to plan it, when you've got to make the effort to drive twenty minutes, you're actually committed to it. you're going to sit there for a couple of hours, have a proper night. you're not just popping in for twenty minutes because you're bored. you've got time to actually talk about things. and the work thing — what you said about dave, nameref — that's it. that's where real conversation happens, i think. you're doing something with your hands, you're not just staring at each other across a table trying to fill the silence. the chat just flows naturally because you're focused on the job. out here, a lot of your friendships are built that way. you help someone with their place, they help you with yours. there's a purpose to it beyond just passing the time. maybe that sounds a bit... i don't know, but i reckon there's something in it. you're not just mates who go to the pub, you're actually useful to each other.

items.speaker: S03
items.quote: yeah. um, yeah, i, i, when you, when you were saying nameref about that, that question three, yeah, i, i would agree with you. i think, um, i think it's males and meat, you know, if i can put it as, if i can put it like that, it, i think, i think, um, i think women are probably more prone to come off meat a lot easier than men. it's just, it's just my opinion. and again, i'm trying to associate with, um, the, um, friends that i go out with. um, i also go out, i mentioned earlier in the discussion that i'll do some invigilating and it's only, it's only about, i don't know, averages throughout the year, um, four or five hours a week, if you take it on an average. um, but i go out with a few of them, the six of us go out every so often and they tend to look less at the meat side of it and they will look more at the the pasta side of it the the vegetarian side of it whereas the the couple of men in there one one is very much a fish and chip man. he comes from south africa. he likes his fish. where i will look at the sort of, the meat side of it, or, or something of that nature, but yeah, i think, i think the gender side of it is certainly, from my point of view, men are meat, definitely.

items.speaker: S03
items.quote: yeah. so, so it's value for money, which is in effect what you're saying. so yeah, yeah, yeah. value for money. and, and i think we've just grown up with the fact that, um, meat's always been in a menu and, um, yeah, again, when you, when you go out nowadays, the price of meat, um, if you, if you want a nice bit of fillet steak, it can be, i suppose it depends where you go, but you'd be lucky to get any change out of 28, 30 pounds, if not more. um, and it's the same with things like ribs and which, which is what i quite like. um, i quite like going out and, um, having some ribs because we don't have them at home. so, so it's a treat every now and again. um, i must admit. i do look at a menu to look at alternatives, but there isn't a great deal that i see that gives me an alternative to what i would normally like, but maybe that that will change in the future after we have these sort of discussions.

items.speaker: S01
items.quote: yeah, it's pretty much the same setup for us, to be honest. my wife does most of the cooking still, and like you say, nameref , she's the one who's got it all in her head — what needs using, what's going off. i couldn't tell you half of what's in the cupboard if you asked me. though i do more of the cooking now than i did when i was working, same as nameref . just because you're there, you might as well. and out here it's the same thing — you can't just pop to the shops whenever, so you've got to work with what you've got. big shop at the weekend, then you're using what's there through the week. the waste thing nameref mentioned — that's real out here. you're not throwing things away because you couldn't be bothered with them. you use what you've got because it costs money to replace it and you can't just nip out. it's practical, that's all. don't really think about it much beyond that, to be honest. you eat what's there, you don't go hungry, and you don't waste things. that's the long and short of it for us.

items.speaker: S04
items.quote: yeah, i'm always, i'm open to trying plant based stuff. it doesn't, you know, i wouldn't, i wouldn't turn my nose, you know, i'm not having that, it’s plant based, you know, unless i've tried it before and i know it's something that i don't enjoy. um, i've tried almond milk, uh, in a coffee, and it's just like, it's just not doing it for me. um, i, you know, i don't think, uh, it would, i think it would only be health related if i was with, um, i'd be, i've, i've, i've dated people who are vegan or, you know, who only eat plant based. and if they're, if they're fine, you know, if, if that's a choice that they've made and they're not kind of, it's not for like kind of ethical reasons. i don't know if i'm articulating that properly but, i could be with someone and i could cook and prepare that food for them no problem at all and i could go with them a little bit on that journey, you know, and share some of that with them. but, equally i enjoy a burger, i enjoy a steak. i wouldn't want to be made to feel bad for my enjoyment of that. um, so if i was with someone that was very much like, your, meat is murder or something like that, i couldn't do it at all. like, you know, that just isn't someone that i could be with. um.

items.speaker: S01
items.quote: yeah, i mean, i think i'd be the same there. i mean, it's, if i'm kind of particularly hungry, then i'll obviously look for something that i consider a bit more filling. um, but if we were in, if i was in the, in the, in the restaurant that we quite often go to, the spanish one obviously, it's it's a tapas bar. so we'll just grab a whole load of different bowls and stuff and we're all mixing and sharing alike. uh, but if we were let's say like yourselves kind of in a pub or a club or something, again, it just comes down to kind of how hungry i am. um. but it would always, i have to admit, it will tend to involve meat. i'm a big meat eater. i'd especially, if i'm, if i'm paying and going out then i like to kind of treat myself to that. i'm not averse to eating vegetarian or or kind of plant based stuff. well not so much plant based. but uh vegetarian meals. but if i'm out i'd like something meaty.

items.speaker: S02
items.quote: yeah, pretty much the same to be honest. there's definitely pubs i just end up in with mates — same thing you lot are saying, you don't really plan it, you just know where people will be. and yeah, we do the curry nights too, loads of decent spots around. i'd probably say the burger thing though, like nameref mentioned — that's a thing for us as well. quick bite, not a massive commitment, but you're still doing something together. and then yeah, when you actually sit down for a proper meal, the conversation's different. you've got time for it. london's got so many spots though that it's kind of... there isn't really one go-to in the same way, i reckon. like, there's always somewhere new or whatever, so it's a bit more varied. but the principle's the same — pub for the routine, somewhere to eat for when you actually want to talk about stuff. that tracks with what you're all saying.

items.speaker: S02
items.quote: i mean... yeah, i think that's actually what i'm doing too, to be honest. because listening to nameref say that out loud, i'm realizing — i'm not saying there's no hook. i'm saying i've clocked that there is one, or there could be, but i'm choosing not to grab it. and i was kind of wrapping that up in "there's no reason to bother," but that's not quite true, is it? like, nameref 's thing about autopilot — i do feel that sometimes. i'll be ordering the same thing, not really thinking about it, and there's that little moment where you go "am i even choosing this or just doing what i've always done?" and it's a bit shit, that feeling. i don't like it. but then i just... don't do anything about it. because actually examining what i'm eating and making a deliberate choice about it feels like it would require me to care about something i'm not currently caring about. and i'm not willing to do that work just to solve a discomfort that i'm already kind of used to, you know? it's not that i don't want to look at myself. it's that i'm looking at myself and going "nah, not worth the friction to change this right now." even though i can feel that the not-changing is a kind of problem. i'm just... accepting it. and maybe that's fair enough, but yeah, nameref 's right — that's different from saying there's no hook. there's definitely a hook. i'm just choosing not to take it.

items.speaker: S05
items.quote: um, yeah, i've thought quite often over the years of whether i could go, um, vegetarian or, vegan i definitely couldn't do. i like dairy too much. but, um, i, i would struggle to go completely plant based just cause i like, i like meat too much. um, i could definitely restrict, reduce my meat intake and perhaps do every other meal or two or three times a week, but then i would start craving some chicken or, or, or steak or something like that. um, no, i would. just enjoyment for me of food, i wouldn't, i wouldn't get so much from eating. so for me to go completely plant based, it would perhaps have to be my health is at risk for some reason, or that i have to be forced to, forced to change perhaps, and change a diet for high cholesterol or something like that.

items.speaker: S02
items.quote: yeah, i think it does actually — but maybe not in the way people usually bang on about, if i'm honest. like, i eat meat regularly. i'm a meat eater. but that's not because i feel like i have to prove something or because it's manly or whatever. it's just what i like. and i reckon that's the thing — being male, you sort of get to just... not think about it too much. you make your choices and no one really questions them. i notice it more when you see other people doing it differently. you'll see someone go vegetarian or whatever, and suddenly everyone's got an opinion about it, you know? all these comments. whereas if i'm just eating a roast on sunday, no one's looking at me sideways about it. no one's saying oh, you're being too manly, or whatever. i think the gender thing is less about what you actually eat and more about the freedom to not have to defend your choices. a bloke can eat meat without anyone making a thing of it. a bloke can also not eat meat, but he might get more... i don't know, pushback maybe? questions about it. whereas a woman eating salad — that's just expected, assumed. or if she eats meat, that's also fair game for comment. so yeah, gender shapes it, but i reckon it's more about the invisibility of it for men. you just do what you do, and it's fine. you don't have to think about what it means about you.

items.speaker: S03
items.quote: yeah, nameref 's got a point about the fairness of it, that's real. i mean, you can see where he's coming from — his wife's already got all that in her head, all that planning, and asking her to take on something completely new on top of that, with no room for error... that's not nothing. but i want to push back a bit on the helplessness of it, if i'm honest. because what i've noticed since i retired is — you don't have to just accept that it all sits on one person. you can actually learn it yourself. i know my wife's got the system in her head, the way she does it. but i've started paying more attention to what she's doing, how she thinks about it. and i could learn it if i wanted to. so if we decided to go plant-based — which we haven't, by the way — i wouldn't just be asking her to work it out and do it. we'd both have to think about it. i'd have to engage with the planning side, not just the cooking. learn what needs to go in the cupboard, what the constraints are, what we can actually get. that's what's changed for me since i retired, really. i've had the time and the headspace to actually pay attention to how my wife manages the whole thing. and i could take some of that on if something changed. i'm not great at it yet, but i could do it. so nameref , i hear you on the fairness thing. but i don't think it has to stay that way. you could start doing more of the planning side yourself. it's not like she's got some magical ability you can't learn.

items.speaker: S04
items.quote: yeah, i think it depends what i'm doing. so like, obviously i'm working in, i'm actually on site in the office. i do normally work hybrid. so i usually go in one or two days a week out of the four days that i work. um, i work in manchester and live on the whirl. so for me, um, tonight, you know, i've planned for the partner that i will just bung a couple of pizzas in, um, because it's a, you know, it takes 10 minutes. then obviously we can actually spend a bit of the time in the evening with our kid. last night because i was at home working, um, i had actually planned out meals. so i'll, i'll try and have a rough plan based around what the schedule for the week is, but um equally i can get home tonight and go, you know, i can't even be assed cooking a pizza. let's order a takeaway because, you know, hour long train journey. so it, it yeah, there's no real plan, um, that we stick to, but i do try to have a bit of a, an idea. but yeah, it's fluid.

items.speaker: S02
items.quote: i think, i think, you know, like gender influences what you eat. if it's like me, we're like, we're like just my guy friends, like we might go somewhere where we know like, there's like cheap beer as well. but nothing, nothing like actual food-wise. i don't think i've ever made a decision on where to eat on like, any influences, like gender-wise. um, so i would say no, for where we would eat.

items.speaker: S01
items.quote: well, it wouldn't happen overnight, would it? it would, you know, it would phase itself out and then farmers or livestock people would stop the breeding processes and, and the populations of the, the herds would drop down to manageable levels where they could live off the land or we could farm them for something else like their, for wool or for their hides or for something else, i suppose.

items.speaker: S02
items.quote: um, yeah. i'd say for me it's probably just the pub, to be honest. nothing fancy — there's a few round where i stay in glasgow that we just end up in regularly. it's easy, you know? you can sit, have a drink, chat about whatever. football, work, what's going on. don't really need to plan it that much. i guess what works about it is it's just... normal. nobody's trying to perform anything or prove anything. you're just there with mates. could be talking about something serious one minute, then someone cracks a joke and you move on. that's kind of it for me.

items.speaker: S01
items.quote: well, for me it's mostly the pub, to be honest. there's one about twenty minutes away — it's nothing fancy, just a proper local. that's where you see the same faces, you know? folk you've known for years. we'll sit there of an evening, have a pint, a chat. it's reliable, that's the thing. you know who you're going to bump into. and then there's the football — i go down to watch when i can. that's another one where you're with the same crowd week in, week out. but if i'm being honest, out where i am, you don't have loads of options for just popping somewhere casual. you've got to make a bit of effort to get anywhere, so when you do go out, you make it count. you're not just wandering down the street to meet someone. it's more deliberate than that, i'd say.

items.speaker: S01
items.quote: yeah, i get that — but i'd say leeds is pretty big, and i still get that same thing, you know? if you find your spot, even in a city, you're not anonymous. it's the same crew most nights. people know you. i think it's more about finding the right pub than the size of the place, if that makes sense. like, there's definitely pubs in leeds where you're just a face in the crowd, but the ones we go to, we're regulars. it's the same vibe you're describing, nameref .

items.speaker: S02
items.quote: yeah, but that's the thing, isn't it — saying "i don't see the point, it doesn't feel like a problem" is kind of the whole thing, nameref . that's exactly the inertia talking. and i get it, i really do. i'm sitting in the same place. but just because something doesn't feel like a problem doesn't mean it isn't one, does it? i mean, we've been talking for forty minutes about how we're not really choosing, we're just doing what we've always done because it's easier. and then when someone points out we could do it differently, we go "yeah, but why would i?" that's... that's the inertia working perfectly, isn't it. it keeps itself going because there's no pressure on it, no reason to question it. and i'm not saying we should all suddenly decide to go plant-based tomorrow or anything. i'm not even sure i believe in that myself. but nameref , you literally said you've noticed yourself buying meat less because of the prices, without consciously deciding to. so something's already shifting whether you think there's a point or not. you're eating less of it. you're just not owning it, or thinking about what that means. for me, i reckon the honest thing is — i could probably eat less meat without it being a drama. my wife could probably figure out some decent plant-based meals if we actually sat down and thought about it. the kids would probably adapt. but none of us are going to do it because it doesn't feel broken, and we're comfortable enough as it is. that's inertia. and yeah, it might be fine. but at least i should be honest about what it actually is.

items.speaker: S02
items.quote: yeah, but i think — i mean, the scrolling thing, that's the bit that gets me. it's not even just about having loads of options, it's that you're doing it on your own, aren't you? on your phone, comparing prices and ratings and looking at photos of the food. like, when you go out with your mates and you're all deciding together, that's different — you're talking about it, someone suggests something, you take the piss out of someone else's choice, whatever. there's a social thing happening. but when you're at home on your own and you're scrolling through deliveroo for twenty minutes, that's... that's just you justifying every choice to yourself. like, why this one and not that one? is this actually good or just well-reviewed? nameref this actually arrive on time? it's exhausting, mate. and that's the thing that's actually changed, i reckon. it's not just about choice — it's that the choice is happening in isolation, on a screen, where you're constantly aware you could pick something else. when there were fewer options and you just went to the chippy or whatever, there was no... there was no endless alternatives sat right there tempting you. i catch myself doing it sometimes and thinking, why am i spending this much mental energy on what to eat? but the app's right there, and all the options are right there, so you kind of have to justify it to yourself, don't you?

items.speaker: S04
items.quote: i take your point, nameref , but i'm wondering if we're maybe mixing two different things up here. there's the pub doing steak nights because that's what sells — that's marketing, that's business. fair enough. but that's not the same as the blokes round the table giving you a hard time for ordering something else, is it? i mean, i've sat with the same group of fellas for years. if one of them decided he wasn't eating meat anymore, would there be a bit of banter? probably, yeah. but that's just how it goes — lads take the piss out of each other about most things. that's not the same as making someone feel unwelcome. and round here, honestly, i'm not sure you'd get the culture you're describing anyway. people are too busy getting on with their lives to worry much about what the bloke next to them is eating. you order your food, nobody comments, you get on with your pint. i suppose what i'm saying is — the themed nights are a marketing thing, that's real enough. but i'm not convinced there's this big social pressure against vegetarians that we're all imposing without realizing it. at least not where i am.

items.speaker: S05
items.quote: yeah, that makes sense. pubs are good for that if you've got them nearby. out where i am though, it's a bit different — the nearest proper pub is like twenty minutes' drive, so you don't just pop in whenever. it's more of a planned thing, you know? usually ends up being someone's house or garden, especially in decent weather. my mate's got a decent setup out back, so we'll just gather there with some beers, bit of a bonfire sometimes. you get the same thing nameref 's talking about — just being able to chat without all the noise — but it's less of a regular spot and more just... whatever works on the day. it's fine, just different i suppose when you're not in town.

items.speaker: S02
items.quote: yeah. we must be doing pretty well, because you said 15 minutes.

items.speaker: S03
items.quote: yeah, okay, fair point. you're right — i was sort of trying to make it all sound fine, wasn't i? but what you're saying is different. you're saying you could do it and you choose not to, which is... that's honest, i think. i mean, i'm the same actually. i do most of my shopping at the supermarket because it's easy, and i know there's an independent butcher not far from me, but i don't really go. not because i can't, just because i don't. it's a choice. and yeah, there's a difference between being busy and just... not bothering, you know? being busy is what it is, but choosing not to bother is on you. thing is, i'm not sure that bothers me that much, to be honest. like, i notice it when meat's done well, but i'm also fine with the supermarket version most of the time. it's not like i'm sacrificing something i really care about. whereas you sound like maybe you do care a bit more about it — like you're noticing the gap between what you could do and what you are doing. which is fair enough, but it's not necessarily a bad thing if you're just choosing convenience and you're okay with that.

items.speaker: S01
items.quote: well, that's the thing, isn't it? out here it's not just a matter of deciding and then doing it. there's logistics to it. i mean, first off, you've got the shop. the co-op's got what it's got. if you wanted proper variety — different plant-based things, alternatives to what you're used to — you'd be driving thirty, forty minutes to get to somewhere that stocks it. or ordering online, which costs you more and takes time. second, and maybe this is just me and how i've lived, but your wife's cooking habits, your social stuff — it all ties into it. if your wife's been cooking the same way for forty years and you suddenly decide you're not eating what she makes, that's not just a food thing, is it? that's a shift in how you do things together. and third — and i've seen this with folk who've tried to change their diet out here — you become a bit of an oddity. not in a kind way necessarily. just... you're the one asking for something different, and there's a cost to that socially. small place, everyone knows what everyone eats. so yeah, theoretically i could decide to go plant-based tomorrow. but practically? you'd need to sort out where you're getting the food, you'd need your household to be on board, and you'd need to be comfortable with standing out a bit. that's all doable. but it's not nothing. it's not just willpower, is it?

items.speaker: S04
items.quote: yeah, that's it exactly. it's familiar because that's what you grew up with — your mum's cooking meat, your dad's cooking meat, that's just what dinner is. and then when you're out with mates, everyone's doing the same thing, so it just becomes... that's normal. that's food. and you're right about the practical side of it too. i know how to cook chicken or a bit of beef, i can do it in half an hour without thinking about it. if i tried to do something else i'd probably have to look it up or figure it out. so there's that inertia as well — you stick with what you know works and tastes decent. i think that's why it doesn't feel like a choice really, even though it is one. because there's nothing pushing you to question it. you're not hungry, you're not broke, nobody's telling you it's a problem. so the choice just becomes... invisible. it's just what you do.

items.speaker: S03
items.quote: yeah, that's fair actually. i hadn't really thought about it like that, but you're right — i've got it easy, haven't i? like, i can just decide what i fancy because there's shops everywhere, multiple options within five minutes. i don't have to plan around anything. whereas what you're describing, you've got to think about it more because the options are actually limited. you can't just pop to a different supermarket if one's not got what you want. so it's more intentional, like you said, but not because you're sitting there philosophising about it — just because that's the reality of where you live. i suppose i do take that for granted a bit. the convenience of just... having options constantly available. for me it's genuinely not a decision most nights, but that's only because i'm in a city where i could literally get anything if i wanted to. doesn't mean i would, but i could. you don't have that, so fair enough it's a different thing for you.

items.speaker: S02
items.quote: fair enough, yeah. you're right — i do notice it when i actually pay attention, i just don't think about it that often. that's different from not caring, i suppose. and yeah, i get what you're saying about picking your spots. i mean, i'll go back to places where the food's decent, same as you lot. if a burger's actually good, you notice it, you remember it. i'm not gonna keep going somewhere that serves rubbish just because it's convenient. i guess the difference is i'm not... i dunno, constantly evaluating where my food's come from or whatever. like, if i'm at tesco grabbing something quick on the way home from work, i'm just grabbing it. but if i'm going out somewhere, yeah, you'd rather go somewhere that's actually put thought into it. it's just different headspaces though, innit? going out is different from just feeding yourself on a tuesday night. i don't need to overthink a weeknight dinner, but when you're going somewhere for a night out with mates, then fair play, might as well be somewhere decent.

items.speaker: S04
items.quote: i think with regards to the last point, we've sort of touched on this in little bits and pieces, but i know obviously one of the things obviously someone said before, texture. i think that's the thing. what's going to make plant based foods more appealing to me, you've got to make it a more, much more like meat or pivot it entirely in the other direction and go, do you know what? and i think, i'm sorry, nameref , it may have been you made this point, but it's actually own the fact that it's not meat. so don't try and package it to be meat.

items.speaker: S03
items.quote: yeah, yeah, yeah. but certainly, as i said, the, the friends that i go out with, um, the male friends that i go out with, i just can't see them going any, any other way, but continuing the way that they are. they don't, um, we don't have a discussion when we go out about, um, what's on the menu or shall we have plant based or anything of that nature. they are, they are slightly, slightly younger than me apart from one of them, um, but they all tend to be, uh, meat eaters and i can't very well see them changing that much. uh, we certainly don't have discussions on plant based food. which is a bit of a shame, but maybe that's just how it is at the minute.

items.speaker: S04
items.quote: yeah, but i think nameref 's being a bit generous there, if i'm honest. because it's not just about how we're reading it — it's actual pressure, isn't it? in a place like ours, if you're doing something different, you're not just standing out. you're under a kind of... scrutiny. people notice, they talk, and that has real consequences for the person doing the thing that's different. i mean, nameref 's right that you notice everything in a small community. but that noticing isn't neutral. if someone regularly orders something without meat, or they're known to be vegetarian, that gets talked about. it becomes a thing about them. and that's not just us reading intention into it — that's us creating actual social pressure around the choice. so when nameref talks about someone making a deliberate choice, i think what he's picking up on is partly that visibility, but it's not just the visibility. it's that in a rural place, being different gets marked. you're aware you're being watched. and that changes how you act, doesn't it? you might eat something different on your own, but in the pub with everyone there, you think twice because you know it'll be noticed and talked about. that's real, i think. it's not just about our interpretation of their intention. it's about how the community actually functions — about what's acceptable and what stands out. and yeah, that does say something about us. but it also says something about the actual constraints people feel when they're doing something different.

items.speaker: S04
items.quote: yeah, that's exactly it, nameref . you've hit on something there. out where i am it's the same — you can't just nip down to the pub round the corner because there isn't one round the corner. so when you do meet up with someone, there's a bit more intention to it, you know? you've actually planned it rather than it just happening. for me it's either down the local, which is a good fifteen, twenty minutes drive, or honestly a lot of it happens at someone's place. someone's kitchen or garage. we'll have a cup of tea, work on something, have a chat. that's actually where quite a bit of the socialising happens out here — you end up at a mate's house because you're already going in that direction or you've arranged to help them with something. the pub's nice when you go, but nameref 's right — it's more of an event. you get yourself ready for it, make the drive. not like you can just pop in for half an hour between other things. and that does change how you do it, i reckon. makes it feel a bit different.

items.speaker: S05
items.quote: no, i don't think that's right, nameref . and i think you're doing what nameref was doing earlier — making it sound more complicated than it actually is. look, i like eating meat. that's a solid thing. i've eaten it for nearly fifty years. i know what it tastes like, how it sits with me, what i'd miss if it wasn't there. that's not dependent on whether it's easy or normal or frictionless. if anything, if i had to defend it or sit with discomfort around it, i'd probably want it more, because i'd have actually thought about why. right now i just... have it. it's there. i enjoy it. but here's what i think you're missing — and this is important — there's a difference between the wanting being shaped by context and the wanting only existing because of context. yeah, sure, if something cost me socially, i might think about it differently. but that's not the same as saying the wanting isn't real without that friction. that's saying if the context changed, how i experience the wanting might change. those are different things. it's like saying you only love your kids because it's easy and normal to love your kids, so if loving them got you grief at the pub, you'd stop wanting to love them. that doesn't make sense. the love is separate from whether it's frictionless. same thing here. i want to eat meat. that wanting is real. it exists independently of whether it's socially easy or difficult. the fact that it happens to be easy doesn't mean the wanting only exists because it's easy. that's just... that's confusing two different things.

items.speaker: S03
items.quote: right, yeah — i think that distinction does change things, doesn't it? like, for me out here, if i actually went plant-based, it wouldn't just be about the thinking bit. it would be completely different practically. i mean, you two are in places where there's shops, there's options, there's... infrastructure for that kind of thing. if i decided tomorrow i was going to eat plant-based, what does that actually look like for me? i'd have to drive somewhere to get the stuff, probably. the village shop doesn't stock half of it. my wife would have to change what she's doing. it would affect everything — shopping, cooking, what's available when you just want to eat without planning it. so for me, it's not just about becoming conscious of it. it's that the whole routine would have to fall apart and then get rebuilt differently. i couldn't just quietly shift into it the way you might be able to. it would have to be a project. a decision i'm making and living with every single day. whereas what nameref 's saying — about losing the ability not to think — that's something else. that's about the loss of ease already being there. he'd be conscious of the change no matter what, because the space where he could just do things is already gone. for me, the change itself would be impossible without basically reorganizing my life. that's a different kind of problem. it's not even really on the table as an option, not practically speaking. and i think that says something about what's been lost out here, doesn't it? not just the ease, but the actual possibility of doing certain things at all.

items.speaker: S05
items.quote: right, okay — so practically speaking, quite a lot actually. like, i know how to cook chicken. i can throw together a stir-fry or a roast or whatever in maybe twenty minutes, and i know it's going to fill me up and taste decent. if i went plant-based, i'd have to... i dunno, learn a whole new set of things, wouldn't i? what actually fills you up? how long do you cook it? what goes with what? and then there's the social side of it. like, if i'm going for a curry with mates on a friday night, there's just... meat curries, innit? everyone orders that. if i suddenly showed up ordering something else, that's a whole conversation you've got to have. you're the one who's different. that's friction. and honestly, at home — i like dairy. cheese, yoghurt, that kind of thing. that's a regular part of how i eat. so going fully plant-based, i'd be cutting that out too, which means even more stuff i'd need to figure out. so yeah, it's not just about deciding you fancy trying it. there's actual practical stuff — learning to cook different things, knowing what works, fitting it around what other people are doing. that's why it just stays as it is, i reckon. it's not because i'm opposed to it or anything. it's just... there's no reason to add all that friction when what i'm doing now works fine.

items.speaker: S01
items.quote: yeah, we've got a slow cooker, actually. i was gonna say we've got six people in the house. um, so, we've kind of got a load of meals that we know everybody, everybody'll eat. and then we tend to batch cook them. i actually work from home most of the time, so i can kind of cook something in the afternoon. but it's really a case of just making these big vats of food that'll last us for a couple of days and just going round with the stuff we know that everyone will eat. so, um, yeah. yeah, it's not the most adventurous.

items.speaker: S03
items.quote: yeah, nameref 's hit on something that i think i've been avoiding a bit, to be honest. all the identity stuff — i was talking about it like it's this big thing, but yeah, the actual friction for me? it's more what he said. it's just... comfortable. i know what i'm doing. i eat chicken most days, red meat once a week, that's just what i do. i know how to cook it, i know where to get it, it takes five minutes. and dairy's the same — cheese on toast, yoghurt in the morning, it's just there. i don't have to think about any of it. if i went plant-based, i'd have to actually learn stuff. work out what tastes decent, spend time on it. and i'm not saying there's anything wrong with that — nameref 's right, it's not a principled reason. it's just... why would i? i'm not uncomfortable with how i eat now. it works fine. the masculinity thing, the defensiveness — yeah, maybe that's in there somewhere too. but honestly, the real reason i'm not going plant-based is just because i can't be bothered to change something that already works. that's the truth of it. and i reckon that's probably more real than all the stuff i was saying before about identity and what it means to be a bloke.

items.speaker: S01
items.quote: that's kind of the same thing though, innit? like, day to day i've got... i mean, there's a tesco round the corner, there's takeaways on every street — chinese, kebab, indian, pizza, whatever. so you'd think that's good, right? but it's actually quite stressful sometimes. like, you'll be hungry and you're stood there scrolling through your phone looking at deliveroo or just eat, and there's literally fifty options, and you're trying to figure out which one's actually decent, which one's not gonna take an hour, which one's not gonna be too pricey. and half the time you end up wasting twenty minutes deciding and then you're still not sure you've made the right choice. and it's the same when you're out with your mates. you'll all be like, right, where we eating? and everyone's got different ideas, and you're looking at reviews, prices, how busy they are... it's supposed to be simpler because there's more choice, but it kind of isn't. you're always thinking, should i go here, or should i try that place instead, or that new one that opened. it's like you can never just... settle on something. whereas i reckon if there was just one or two decent spots you knew, you'd just go there and not think about it. you'd know what you're getting. but when there's that much choice it's almost paralyzing, you know? like, any decision you make feels like you're missing out on something better.

items.speaker: S02
items.quote: yeah, i'd say as well, time is quite a big factor in terms of, um, what you eat in some ways, because like, not so much a problem for now, because i'm a teacher, but during like school term time, staff meeting night, wednesday, it's always long. so i don't really want to be spending ages cooking. or like, i mean, if i'm running a sports club or something after school, so i might make something like, i don't know, say like a tuna pasta bake, which i know is going to last a couple of nights or whatever. so if i know i've got a busy night coming, and i'm not going to get back till late, i'll do, uh, deliberately do something maybe the day or so before, which i know is just going to still be there. i can bung it in the microwave for three minutes or whatever, and then after a long day, you really don't have to spend that long faffing about, you know.

items.speaker: S03
items.quote: so, so nameref in terms of you going on the plant based, was it something you said i'm going on a plant based, sort of, um, food regime or you just decided to cut out the meat or did you specifically go for the plant based, um, type of food?

items.speaker: S01
items.quote: yeah, and again, i don't know. i'm sure i'm not just being kind of cynical about this, but i just, i, i mean, certainly within my social group, the men aspect of it is just a, just a, we wouldn't even consider it being kind of unmanly. if one of our mates walked in with a plant based burger, i'm not going to start ribbing him for it. i mean, that's his choice. so it's, my choice again, doesn't come down to, to being anything to do with being a man or male and any sort of macho, or unmacho, uh, vision that i might have of being plant based. i think. i think those days are long gone, where people thought of vegetarians as kind of weak, hippie, airy fairy sorts of people. uh, that, that, society's changed now.

items.speaker: S04
items.quote: right, yeah. well — the pub, to be honest. that's where i see the lads mostly. there's one just off the main road, nothing fancy, but it's got a good mix of people and they don't mind you sitting there for a couple of hours on a saturday afternoon. you can actually hear each other talk, which sounds daft but you'd be surprised how many places you can't. i've got mates i've known since school — a few of them are still local, some have drifted further out, but when they're back in the area that's where we end up. you don't have to plan much, just... you know where people will be. there's a darts board, there's sky sports on if there's a match on, but mostly it's just the talking really. and i get what you lot were saying just then about the embedded thing. i mean, i hadn't thought about it quite like that before, but yeah — knowing where you belong, where people know you. i don't see my old man as much as i probably should, he's about twenty minutes away still, but that's sort of in the back of my mind too, you know? that he's settled where he is, people know him. that matters.

items.speaker: S02
items.quote: yeah, that's a good point nameref made about the markup. i've actually noticed that sometimes — like, you'll hear what someone's paying a farmer for beef, and then you see what a restaurant's charging for it, and it's mad, innit? the difference between what the person producing it gets and what you end up paying. i mean, i'm not gonna pretend i'm thinking about that every time i grab something from tesco, because honestly i'm not. but when you do notice it, it's a bit mad. like, the farmer's getting paid next to nothing and then somehow it's fifteen quid for a burger on a menu. that's probably why a lot of pubs just stick with the standard suppliers though — easier to know what you're gonna pay, easier to manage. building those relationships like you're doing, nameref , that takes time and effort that most places probably can't be bothered with. even if it'd be better for them in the end.

items.speaker: S03
items.quote: i mean... i do most of the cooking myself, so it's different from nameref 's setup. but i think some of what he's saying still applies, just in a different way. i've got a set of meals that work — a roast on sunday, bit of chicken midweek, fish when i fancy it. i know how to do those, they're not a production. if i was going to change all that, yeah, i'd need to learn new ways of doing things. that takes time, and honestly, at my age i'm not sure i've got the energy to faff about with a load of new recipes that might not work out. but nameref 's right about something — there is a different bar for changing away from what you're already doing. like, i eat meat most days without thinking about it. if someone said "what if you didn't?" i'd probably think of all the reasons why it wouldn't work rather than just... trying it. that's fair. thing is though, i'm not entirely sure what i'd be changing for. i'm not convinced it's something i actually need to do. so yeah, i could probably eat less meat, and like i said, the prices have pushed me in that direction anyway. but going properly plant-based? i don't think that's something i'm going to do. not because it's impossible or anything, just... i don't see the point for me personally. i like what i eat, it works, and i haven't got a strong reason to change it. maybe that's just inertia too, like nameref said. probably is, if i'm being honest. but it doesn't feel like a problem from where i'm sitting.

items.speaker: S01
items.quote: well, the infrastructure thing is different where i am, isn't it? out here, there's not much of an option at all, if i'm being honest. you go to the pub, you get what's on the menu — usually a steak, a pie, maybe fish and chips. there's not a plant-based option sitting there waiting. and the supermarket twenty miles away, they've got some stuff, but it's not like you're spoiled for choice. so if i decided to go plant-based tomorrow, i'd not just be dealing with the awkwardness — i'd be dealing with the fact that there's nowhere to eat out, and i'd be doing a lot of driving to get the ingredients. that's a real barrier, not just a psychological one. it's not just comfort, it's practicality. but listening to nameref and nameref ... i think nameref 's got something there about the time thing not really being an excuse. i'm sixty-four. i could have another twenty, thirty years. that's not insignificant. and if i'm sitting here saying i've been complicit in keeping this thing going because it didn't inconvenience me, well... at some point you've got to decide if that bothers you enough to actually do something about it. the thing is though, i don't know if i have that pull that nameref 's got. he's decided he wants to do it differently. i haven't really got to that point. i eat meat, i'm not against it, i'm not struggling with it. so the question for me isn't really about infrastructure or time — it's whether i actually want to change. and i'm not sure i do, not enough to be bothered with all of it. which means i'm probably just going to keep doing what i'm doing, and that's... yeah, that's complicit, like i said earlier. but at least now i'm seeing it clearly.

items.speaker: S02
items.quote: nameref , i hear you saying that, and i think you're being honest. but i want to push back a bit on something. because the way you're framing it — like, you've just talked about things and i've actually done something — it sounds like the difference is just willpower, right? like, you should have just decided and done it. but that's not quite what's happened for me. the thing is, me and my wife — we didn't just decide one day that we'd cook together one night a week and suddenly it happened. there was friction. there was real friction. like, we've both been tired, we've both got habits, and changing that takes... it's not easy. it's still not easy, to be honest. what's different isn't that i'm more committed than you are. it's that we actually ran into the friction and kept going anyway. we had the conversation, yeah, but then we tried it and some nights it was shit because we were exhausted and we half-arsed it. and some nights it's worked. but we're still in the middle of it, we're still figuring it out. so when you're listening to me and thinking, right, i need to just decide and do that — i think that's missing what actually happened. it's not about deciding harder. it's about being willing to run into the friction and not give up when it's uncomfortable or when it doesn't work the first few times. that's the bit i think matters, not the commitment part. it's the friction part.

items.speaker: S04
items.quote: yeah, i mean... it's a bit of both, innit? like, with my thursday lads, i've known most of them for ages, so it's pretty relaxed. i'll order what i want, no one's bothered. but nameref 's right that i probably still do sometimes just go for something dead normal because it's easier, you know? not because i think they'll care, just because... it's what you do. but then nameref 's point about context — that's real too. like, if we're out and someone's brought someone new, or we're in a bigger group, yeah, there's a bit of that awareness. you're not going to order something mad and then spend ten minutes explaining what it is or why you're having it. i suppose the thing i'm thinking about is what nameref said about testing that stuff with your actual mates. because i've not really... i don't think i've tested it much, have i? i just kind of know what i normally order and i stick with it. whether that's because i genuinely prefer it or because i'm just used to not ordering other things, i couldn't really tell you. with the kids thing we were talking about earlier, though — it's making me wonder if i'll have more of that awareness creep in, you know? because once you've got a kid, you're around different people more. parents, that sort of thing. and maybe you care a bit more about how you come across because it's not just your mates anymore.

items.speaker: S02
items.quote: yeah, that's it exactly. that's what i was trying to get at. nameref 's nailed it. because nameref , you keep coming back to the constraint creating something real, and i'm not arguing it doesn't. but you're also suggesting that because i've got options, what i've got is somehow less solid or less committed. and that's not it at all. i choose to go back to the same places. i choose to see the same people. that's deliberate. and yeah, if it went wrong — if the pub got dodgy or the bloke at the shop was a pain — i could go somewhere else. but i haven't needed to, because it works. that's not a weakness in what i've got. that's just... it's actually functioning properly. i think there's a difference between being locked in and choosing to stay. you're locked in, nameref . you've made the best of it and fair play to you. but i'm not locked in. i'm choosing it. and i don't think that means my relationships or my patterns are any thinner than yours. they're just not constrained by geography in the same way. nameref 's right — they're different kinds of real. yours is forced to work. mine is choosing to keep working. neither one's automatically stronger.

items.speaker: S02
items.quote: that's up to individual preference though, isn't it? two years ago, i went on a plant based diet. okay, yeah. i lost three stone in two years, which is, i suppose, okay. i don't know. but i eat meat once in a blue moon now. one, because it's really expensive. two, i find it hard to cook. so i decided to go plant based 95 percent of the time and to cook your own food it's very easy to do and it's quick and i would recommend it to anybody if they can make that change.

items.speaker: S03
items.quote: for me it's pretty straightforward, honestly. i eat meat most nights — red meat couple times a week, bit of chicken, fish now and then. it's just... that's what i cook. don't really overthink it. like, i'll come home from work, think about what i fancy, and it's usually something with meat in it. sometimes it's what's in the fridge, sometimes i've planned it a bit. but it's not like i'm weighing up options or anything — it's just habit, i suppose. what my family ate growing up, what i've always done. it works for me. dairy i'm less bothered about, to be honest. i don't really think about that side of things. just eat it if it's there, doesn't really matter to me either way.

items.speaker: S01
items.quote: yeah, similar sort of thing really. i eat meat most days — red meat couple times a week, fish when i fancy it, bit of chicken. that's just what i'm used to, what i cook. cost definitely matters, especially the last couple of years with everything going up. you notice the meat prices more because like nameref said, it's a bigger bit of the bill. but honestly, i haven't shifted what i'm eating that much. maybe i'm picking up different cuts if something's on offer, but i'm not thinking, "right, i'll eat less meat" or anything. it's just... you work with what's there and what you can afford that week. some weeks maybe i'm having it a bit less, but that's not some conscious decision i'm making. the thing is though — and i don't know if this is just me — but i think people make a bigger deal out of this stuff than they need to. you get all this talk about, you know, eating less meat, being more conscious about it, and fair enough if that's what someone wants to do. but you've got blokes down the pub saying they'd never give it up, making out it's some sort of threat or whatever, and on the other side you've got people acting like you're doing something wrong if you eat a steak. it's just food, isn't it. you eat what you like, what works for you. doesn't need to be some big statement about it either way.

items.speaker: S01
items.quote: okie dokie. um, well, mine is, if i was meeting up with a group of friends, i suppose obviously, it depends on the occasion. um, but if i was going out for a meal for it, for example, um, we've got a particularly nice spanish restaurant which we all enjoy. so it's a tapas, got a great atmosphere, it kind of transports you to feel that you're there, it's kind of one of those kind of very atmospheric kind of dark moody lighting sort of place. so we always have a good laugh in there. it's a good good place to share and and just be able to chat as well because it's not too noisy.

items.speaker: S04
items.quote: yeah, that local thing nameref mentioned — i get that. it's a bit similar where i'm from, actually. like, knowing the butcher or going to the same place — that's still a thing in a lot of northern ireland. you know who you're buying from, there's a relationship there, it matters to people. but i'd say it's slightly different from what you're describing, nameref . it's not really about a broader food culture or caring about provenance in the way you mean it. it's more just... that's how you've always done it. your da went to the butcher, you go to the butcher. it's local because it's what's there, not necessarily because anyone's made a conscious choice about supporting local farms or whatever. it's just the practical thing, and it happens to be local. but yeah, like nameref and nameref said — for me it's the same really. meat most days, chicken's the easy one, red meat couple times a week. eggs, dairy here and there. i don't overthink it. it's just what you eat. i grew up with it, everyone around you eats like that, so that's normal. you don't sit around examining it — you just make dinner.

items.speaker: S05
items.quote: honestly, i'm in a bit of the same boat as nameref , i think. i've got a couple of pubs i'll go to, but i wouldn't say i'm really a regular anywhere in that way nameref is describing. and yeah, part of it is the commuter thing — i'm knackered when i get home most days, especially if the trains have been a nightmare, and by the time you've dealt with the family and everything, the last thing you want to do is organize going out somewhere. but i think nameref 's actually onto something there about just deciding to commit to it. i mean, i could probably make more of an effort. there's a pub literally ten minutes from my house i quite like — decent enough place, decent people in there — and i could just... go more regularly, couldn't i? just make it a thing instead of saying i'll pop down when i get a chance and then never quite doing it. the difference with nameref i suppose is he's built that up over years, so it's just automatic now. but you're right that it needs the initial push. i think for us in the commuter belt it's just harder to get that momentum going because life's so fractured anyway — you're commuting out, you're commuting back, and then you're just tired. that said, i do see some of the lads from work quite a bit. we'll grab a pint after work sometimes, but that's different, isn't it? that's more... convenient, because you're already out. not the same as having your local spot where you've actually built something.

items.speaker: S02
items.quote: so you're, but what you're not saying is that if the meat is cheaper than the, the veg, then the, the, yeah, the plant based food, you'll have the meat. because it's cheaper.

items.speaker: S05
items.quote: yeah, that's exactly it. and i think that's the bit that gets to me, honestly. because you can sit there and go, well, there's still food, there's still apps, you've got options — and technically that's true. but the actual... the actual texture of it, you know? that's gone. like, i used to know the woman who ran the takeaway i mentioned. not well, but you'd go in and she'd remember what you usually ordered, chat for a minute. and now it's just... you tap your phone and forty minutes later a driver you'll never meet again leaves it on your step. you don't know who made it. you've got no connection to it at all. and that feeds into what we were saying about community earlier, doesn't it? because it's not just about having a pub where you bump into mates. it's that all these small interactions, the ones that made a place feel like an actual place, they're just... they're gone. and you don't realise how much you miss them until they're not there anymore. the transactional bit is the thing. everything's efficient now, and i get why that's meant to be better, but it's also kind of cold. you're not part of anywhere. you're just a customer moving through the system. and the worst part is, like nameref said, you don't even properly notice it's happening because the app's making it look like there's still loads going on. but there isn't, not really.

items.speaker: S01
items.quote: yeah, i reckon it does, but maybe not in the way people sometimes make it sound, you know? like, there's definitely something about... when you're growing up, the men in your family are eating a certain way, and that becomes what normal is. your dad's having his meat and potatoes, that's dinner. your mates are all doing the same thing. so you're picking that up just from being around it. but i don't know if it's... i mean, i eat meat because i like it and it's practical, not because i'm trying to prove i'm a bloke or anything. that's what i'm a bit skeptical about, when people go on about meat being this masculine thing. like, it's just food, innit? but yeah, the fact that i grew up in a household where the men were eating meat, and all my mates do — there's definitely something there. it shapes what feels normal. i suppose with the curry nights and stuff i mentioned earlier, there's probably gender in that too — it's a thing you do with your mates, it's part of being a man in your twenties and thirties, going out with the lads. but that's more about... the routine of it, who you're with, than the food itself. does that make sense?

items.speaker: S01
items.quote: yeah, it's an expensive process eating out and, illogical this may sound, um, if i'm looking at a menu and it's got a vegetarian dish for, let's say 16 or 17 pounds, i just found it off putting. i think, but you know, i understand meat being that much, but veg it can't be. i know that's illogical.

items.speaker: S01
items.quote: right, yeah. i mean, honestly? it's a bit of a mix. during the week i'm working, so it's quick — chicken, pasta, whatever i can throw together in twenty minutes. i'm not thinking too hard about it. but i've got a bit more flexibility than nameref in that my wife works as well, so we kind of share it — sometimes i'll cook, sometimes she does, and we just sort of decide on the day based on what we fancy and what we've got in. the difference i suppose is i can pop to tesco when i need something, or if we fancy a specific meal we'll just get what we need. there's loads of choice. but to be honest, we probably go to the same couple of supermarkets most of the time anyway, and we've got our regular places we'll eat out at — like we'll go back to the same restaurants or pubs we know are decent. so i'm not sure i'm that different from what you two are saying, really. i've got choice, yeah, but in practice i'm probably doing the same things most weeks. i'm not sitting there going right, let me explore every option available in manchester. that would be exhausting. you settle into a rhythm because it's easier, innit. whether that's because you've got to or because you can't be bothered to change it — i mean, the end result's probably pretty similar.
